name: Husqvarna Classic Chainsaw Chaps
title: Husqvarna Classic Chainsaw Chaps: Fit, Sizing & Care
meta: Husqvarna chainsaw chaps in a classic apron style for ground work, bucking and storm cleanup. How to size them, wear them and know when to retire a pair.
tagline: Apron-style leg protection for ground sawing, bucking and cleanup crews.
summary: The Husqvarna Classic is a straightforward pair of Husqvarna chainsaw chaps built for ground work: felling, bucking and limbing brush on cleanup jobs. They buckle over your regular work pants, so you can pull them on at the truck and drop them when you switch to the chipper.
highlights: Apron-style chaps that wear over your own work pants
Layered cut-resistant fibers across the front of the legs
Adjustable waist and leg straps for a snug, no-flap fit
Good fit for ground crews, homeowners and storm cleanup
Easy to take on and off between saw work and other tasks
specs: Waist belt and leg straps with buckles

p: Chaps only work if they cover the right area. Pick a length that reaches to about 2 inches above the top of your boot when you stand straight, and cinch the leg straps so the panels do not swing open when you step over a log. Loose chaps catch brush and slide around, which leaves the inside of the knee exposed.

Husqvarna chaps are a good everyday pair for ground crews that buck and limb behind the climber. If you run a saw most of the day or work in hot weather, compare them with chainsaw pants, which move better on long days.

body.h: Inspection and when to retire them
p: The protective layers inside work by pulling fibers into the chain and stopping it. Once a chain has cut into the outer shell and pulled fibers, that area is done and the chaps should be replaced, not patched. Check the label for the standard they are certified to and follow the manufacturer's washing instructions, since fuel, bar oil and dirt break down the fibers over time.
Chaps reduce the chance of a serious leg cut, but they do not make a saw safe. Keep two hands on the saw, use proper stance and footing, and get trained before you run a chainsaw on a job.

faq.q: What length Husqvarna chaps should I buy?
faq.a: Measure from your belt line to about 2 inches above your boot top while standing. Choose the length closest to that measurement so the chaps cover your shins without dragging.

faq.q: Can I wash chainsaw chaps?
faq.a: Usually yes, by hand or on a gentle cycle per the care label. Do not use bleach or high heat, and let them air dry.

name: Clogger DefenderPro Light Chainsaw Pants
title: Clogger DefenderPro Light Chainsaw Pants: Buying Guide
meta: Clogger chainsaw pants built light for climbing and long ground days. See how the DefenderPro Light fits, breathes and protects, and who it suits best.
tagline: Lightweight, breathable chainsaw pants for climbers and hot-weather ground work.
summary: The DefenderPro Light is the Clogger chainsaw pants option for people who want saw protection without the bulk. It is cut for climbing, walking brush piles and working in heat, with the protective layers built into the front of the leg instead of strapped on top.
highlights: Lightweight build aimed at climbers and warm-weather work
Protective layers built into the front of the legs
Stretch panels for high steps, ladder work and climbing
Venting to help on long, hot days
Trousers style, so nothing flaps or snags like loose chaps
specs: Climbing, hot weather, all-day saw use

body.h: Why climbers like Clogger DefenderPro pants
p: Most chainsaw protection is heavy, and that weight is what makes people leave it in the truck. The DefenderPro Light is Clogger's answer for the climber who runs a top-handle saw all day and the ground person who is moving fast through a big storm job. It is cut close enough to climb in, with stretch where your knees and hips bend.

Because the protection is part of the pants, there are no straps to adjust and nothing to swing into brush. You get dressed once in the morning and you are covered whether you are in the canopy, feeding the chipper or bucking wood at the landing.

Weight matters more aloft than on the ground. Every extra pound on your legs is something you lift on every footlock, every step up a spur climb and every reposition in the crown. Light pants also dry faster after a rainy morning or a sweaty afternoon, which keeps them from chafing by the end of the day.

Like other chainsaw pants, the front panels use layers of long cut-resistant fibers. If a moving chain contacts the leg, the fibers pull out and jam the sprocket to stop the chain. That only works in the protected zone, so know where it is on your pants: the front of the legs. The back of the leg is not protected.

Check the label for the standard and protection class the pants are certified to, and buy the class that matches your saw work and your employer's requirements. Any cut through the outer fabric into the protective layer means the pants are done. Replace them; do not sew up a damaged panel and keep working.

No chainsaw pants are cut-proof. A saw running at full throttle with a sharp chain can cut through any protective layer if it hits hard enough, and the protection does nothing for a slow, grinding contact with a stalled chain. Treat the pants as a last line of defense behind good saw handling, solid work positioning and a chain brake you actually use.

Chaps are cheaper and easy to take off, which suits occasional saw use. Lightweight chainsaw pants cost more but are cooler, move better and stay put, which matters when you are climbing or running a saw most of the day. Many crews keep a pair of chainsaw chaps on the truck for occasional users and put full-time sawyers in pants.
If you want something tougher for heavy brush and logging, look at Clogger's other models. If heat and mobility are your main complaints, the DefenderPro Light is the one to try first.

Order your normal waist size and check the leg length so the protective panel reaches the boot top without bunching. Wash them per the care label, keep bar oil and fuel off them where you can, and inspect the front panels after every job. PPE helps, but training, saw handling and good footing are what keep you out of trouble.

Keep a second pair if you work every day. Rotating pants lets one pair dry and get washed while you wear the other, and it means a damaged pair can be retired right away instead of being worn "just until Friday". Write the purchase date inside the waistband so you can track how long each pair lasts in your work.

faq.q: Are Clogger DefenderPro Light pants good for climbing?
faq.a: Yes. They are designed to be light and flexible, with stretch panels that make high steps and climbing more comfortable than heavier saw pants or chaps.

faq.q: Do lightweight chainsaw pants protect as well as heavy ones?
faq.a: Protection depends on the standard and class printed on the label, not the weight alone. Compare the certification of each model and match it to your saw work.

faq.q: Can I repair a cut in my chainsaw pants?
faq.a: No. If a chain has cut into the protective layer, replace the pants. Small tears in the outer fabric that do not reach the protective layer can be checked against the manufacturer's guidance.

faq.q: How do I wash Clogger chainsaw pants?
faq.a: Follow the care label. In general, wash on a gentle cycle without bleach or fabric softener and let them dry without high heat.

name: Clogger Denim Chainsaw Pants
title: Clogger Denim Chainsaw Pants: Fit, Protection & Care
meta: Denim chainsaw pants from Clogger that look like work jeans but carry built-in saw protection. Fit, care and how they compare with chaps and logger pants.
tagline: Saw protection in a work-jean look for crews, homeowners and firewood cutters.
summary: These Clogger denim chainsaw pants put saw protection inside a pair of pants that look and wear like work jeans. They suit ground crews, firewood cutters and anyone who wants to stay protected without strapping on chaps every time they pick up a saw.
highlights: Denim outer for a work-jean look and abrasion resistance
Cut-protective layers built into the front of the legs
No straps or buckles to adjust between tasks
Comfortable for ground work, bucking and firewood days
Wears well in cooler weather and dirty, scratchy brush
specs: Ground work, bucking, firewood, cooler weather

body.h: Chainsaw pants that look like work jeans
p: Plenty of people who run a saw a few days a week do not want to look like they are dressed for a logging show. Clogger's denim chainsaw pants solve that. From a few feet away they read as heavy work jeans, but the front of each leg carries layered cut-resistant material that is designed to stop a moving chain.

That makes them handy for owner-operators who bid jobs, run the chipper and buck wood all in one day, and for homeowners cutting firewood who would rather not deal with chaps. Old loggers pants were just tough canvas or wool. These are saw pants with real protection.

body.h: Where they fit on a tree crew
p: On a typical removal, the ground person is limbing, bucking rounds and dragging brush for hours. Denim chainsaw pants hold up well to that kind of scraping and stay in place without straps. In cooler months they are comfortable all day.
In hot weather or for climbing, a lighter pair such as the Clogger DefenderPro Light will be cooler and move better. If you only run a saw now and then, chaps may be the cheaper answer.

They also make sense for the climber who comes down to help clean up. Rather than swapping into chaps for an hour of bucking, a climber who wears denim saw pants on cool days stays covered from the first cut to the last load of chips.

Check the label for the standard and class the pants are certified to, and confirm they meet what your employer or contract requires. Protection only covers the marked zone on the front of the legs, so keep the saw away from the back of your legs and your feet.

Inspect the pants after each job. If a chain has cut through the denim into the protective layer, retire them. Fuel and bar oil soak into fibers and can reduce performance, so wash them per the care label and do not let them sit saturated.

Denim also takes more abuse from stubs, bark and blackberry than thin technical fabrics, but it holds more water and dries slowly. On wet days the pants get heavy, so hang them to dry overnight rather than leaving them balled up in the truck.

body.h: Buying chainsaw pants for sale online
p: Order by waist size and inseam, and try them on with the boots you work in. The protective panel should reach the top of your boot when you are standing and stay there when you kneel. Pants that are too long bunch and drag; too short leaves a gap at the shin. Whatever you buy, saw training, good stance and two hands on the saw matter more than any fabric.

Think about how much you actually run a saw before you spend. Daily sawyers get the most value from good chainsaw pants because they are wearing protection all day anyway. If you saw for an hour a month, a pair of chaps over your regular jeans is a reasonable choice.

faq.q: Are denim chainsaw pants as safe as regular chainsaw pants?
faq.a: Safety comes from the certified protective layers, not the outer fabric. Check the label for the standard and protection class, and compare it with any other pair you are considering.

faq.q: Can I wear Clogger denim pants in summer?
faq.a: You can, but denim is warmer than lightweight saw pants. Many sawyers switch to a lighter model for hot weather and keep denim for cooler months.

faq.q: What is the difference between loggers pants and chainsaw pants?
faq.a: Traditional loggers pants are just tough work pants. Chainsaw pants include cut-protective layers designed to stop a moving chain, which plain work pants do not have.

name: Clogger Zero Gen 2 Chainsaw Pants
title: Clogger Zero Gen 2 Chainsaw Pants: Light Saw Protection
meta: Clogger Zero Gen 2 chainsaw pants are built very light for climbers and hot days. How they fit, how they protect and how they compare with logging pants.
tagline: Very light chainsaw pants for climbers and sawyers who work in heat.
summary: The Zero Gen 2 is the Clogger pair aimed at people who want the lightest possible saw protection. It is a favorite style with climbers and summer storm crews who run a saw all day and need pants that breathe and stretch.
highlights: Lightweight design for climbing and hot weather
Protective layers built into the front of the legs
Stretch fabric for big steps and climbing moves
Second-generation update to the Zero line
Trouser style with no straps to snag

body.h: What the Clogger Zero line is for
p: Clogger built the Zero range around one idea: saw protection people will actually wear. Heavy logging pants and chaps work, but in July they turn into a sweat bag and end up behind the seat. The Zero Gen 2 cuts weight and adds stretch so you can climb, crawl through brush and move logs without fighting your clothes.
Climbers using a top-handle saw are the obvious fit. Ground people on long removals and storm crews running saws for days in a row get the same benefit.

The Gen 2 update keeps the same idea as the original Zero and refines the fit and materials. If you wore the first generation and liked it, the second generation is meant to feel familiar while addressing the feedback climbers gave on the first round.

The front of each leg has layered cut-resistant fibers designed to clog the drive sprocket and stop the chain when it contacts the pants. Clogger also offers Zero chaps for people who prefer to strap protection over their own pants. Either way, protection only covers the front of the legs.

Read the label for the certification standard and protection class, and make sure it matches your saw work and your employer's rules. A chain cut into the protective layer means it is time for new pants.

No pants are cut-proof. Protection is designed to stop a chain at the speeds and conditions in the standard, and it does nothing if the saw contacts an unprotected area. Your first defense is still saw handling: chain brake on when you move, two hands on the saw, and a secure work position before you cut.

body.h: Clogger Zero vs heavier logging pants
p: Heavier logging pants usually have tougher outer fabric and hold up better to constant blackberry, rock and stump abrasion. The Zero Gen 2 gives up some of that toughness for comfort and mobility. For felling and bucking in rough country, a heavier pant may last longer. For climbing and hot weather, the Zeros are easier to live with.
Compare them with the Clogger DefenderPro Light if you want a middle ground between weight and durability.

Climbers should also think about how the pants work with a saddle. Leg loops and bridges sit over the upper thigh, so look for a cut that does not bunch under the leg straps. Light, stretchy fabric generally rides under a saddle better than stiff heavy pants.

Order your usual waist size, and check inseam so the protective panel meets your boot top. Wash them per the label without bleach or softener. Inspect after each day on the saw, keep fuel and oil off them, and remember that pants back up good technique, they do not replace it. Get trained before running a saw on the job.

Because light pants trade some abrasion resistance for comfort, expect them to show wear sooner if you spend a lot of time kneeling on rough wood or dragging brush. Many sawyers keep the Zeros for climbing days and hot weather and a tougher pair for heavy ground work.

faq.q: Are Clogger Zeros good for climbing?
faq.a: Yes. The Zero line is built light with stretch, which makes it one of the more comfortable options for climbers running a top-handle saw.

faq.q: What is the difference between Clogger Zero pants and Zero chaps?
faq.a: The pants have protection built in and replace your work pants. The chaps strap over your own pants and come off quickly when you stop sawing.

faq.q: How long do Clogger chainsaw pants last?
faq.a: It depends on how hard you work them. Retire them right away after any chain contact that reaches the protective layer, and replace them when the outer fabric wears through.

name: Eagle Green Safety Can
title: Eagle Green Safety Can for Bar Oil and Combustibles
meta: An Eagle safety can in green for storing and carrying oil and other combustibles on the truck. How metal safety cans work and how to set up your fuel kit.
tagline: Metal safety can in green to keep oil and combustibles separate from gas on the truck.
summary: This Eagle safety can is a metal container in green, the color many crews use to mark oil or other combustibles so nobody pours the wrong thing into a saw. It is a solid upgrade from a plastic jug rolling around the truck bed.
highlights: Metal safety can with spring-closing lid
Green color helps separate oil or combustibles from gasoline
Carry handle for pouring with one hand
Built to ride in a truck box or on a trailer
Common choice for shops, crews and fleets

body.h: Why use a metal safety can
p: Plastic jugs are cheap, but they crack, leak and swell in the sun. A metal Eagle safety can has a spring-loaded lid that closes on its own and vents pressure, so it does not puff up on a hot afternoon. It also stands up to being bumped around a truck box all season.
On a tree crew, fluids get handled all day: topping off saws, refilling bar oil and fueling the chipper. Having proper cans for each fluid keeps the truck cleaner and cuts down on mix-ups.

Eagle has been making safety cans for a long time, and their cans are a common sight in tree service shops, municipal yards and fleet garages. Parts such as lids and gaskets are widely available, which helps a can last for years.

A good can also makes refueling faster. A wide, steady pour from a can with a proper spout means less oil down the side of the saw and on the ground, and less time spent wiping up before you get back to work.

Colors on safety cans are a convention, not a law of nature, but most shops follow something close to this: red for gasoline, yellow for diesel, blue for kerosene and green for oil or other combustibles. Pick a system, label every can and stick to it. Pouring diesel or bar oil into a saw tank costs a lot more than a can.
Many crews keep a green can for bar and chain oil and a red can for mixed fuel. For premix, see Husqvarna 2-stroke premix fuel.

Write the contents on the can in large letters as well. Colors fade, and new crew members do not always know your system. A simple paint-pen label that says BAR OIL or MIX 50:1 heads off mistakes on a busy morning.

Keep the can upright and secured in the truck so it cannot tip or slide. Fill it outdoors, away from running engines and sparks, and do not overfill: leave room for expansion. Check the label for the rated contents and any listings, and use the can only for what it is marked for.
Inspect the lid gasket and spring now and then. If the lid no longer snaps shut or the gasket is cracked, replace the part or the can. Store full cans out of direct sun when the truck is parked.

Plan where the cans ride. A rack or a strap point in the truck bed or utility body keeps them upright and away from the chipper exhaust and hot saws. Keep spill rags and a small absorbent kit nearby so a drip at the fill point does not become a mess in the truck box.

Remember that fuel and oil vapors are the real hazard. Never fill cans in an enclosed trailer, never smoke around them, and ground metal cans when filling from a larger tank if your shop procedure calls for it.

faq.q: What does a green safety can mean?
faq.a: Green is commonly used for oil or other combustible liquids, not gasoline. Label the can with its contents so everyone on the crew knows what is in it.

faq.q: Can I put gasoline in a green safety can?
faq.a: Use the can only for the liquids it is rated and labeled for. Most crews keep gasoline in red cans so there is no confusion.

faq.q: Why is a metal can better than a plastic jug?
faq.a: A metal safety can has a self-closing lid, holds up to rough handling and vents pressure instead of swelling in the heat.

name: Husqvarna 2-Stroke Premix Fuel, 4.75 Gallon
title: Husqvarna 50:1 Pre-Mix 2-Stroke Fuel, 4.75 Gallon
meta: Husqvarna 50:1 pre-mix 2-stroke fuel in a 4.75 gallon container. Ethanol-free premixed fuel for saws, blowers and trimmers that sit between jobs.
tagline: Ethanol-free 50:1 premixed fuel in a bulk size for crews running several saws.
summary: Husqvarna 50:1 pre-mix 2-stroke fuel comes ready to pour, with oil already blended in at the right ratio. This 4.75 gallon size is aimed at crews and heavy users who want consistent fuel for every saw, blower and trimmer on the truck.
highlights: Premixed at 50:1, ready to pour
Ethanol-free fuel that stores better than pump gas
Bulk 4.75 gallon size for crews and fleets
Takes mixing errors out of the equation
Good for equipment that sits between jobs

p: Pump gas with ethanol picks up water, goes stale and gums up carburetors, especially in saws that only come out for storm work. Premixed 2-stroke fuel is ethanol-free and already blended with oil, so it stores better and every tank gets the same mix.

On a crew, mixing is where mistakes happen. Someone forgets the oil, doubles it, or uses the wrong ratio from a different machine. A sealed container of Husqvarna premix removes that variable. Top-handle saws, big felling saws and blowers all get the same fuel.

Premix also helps with equipment that runs only a few times a year: the pole saw, the backup blower, the big felling saw that comes out for the occasional large removal. Running those machines on fuel that does not go stale makes them more likely to start when you need them.

body.h: Is the bulk size worth it
p: Quart cans are handy for homeowners and for keeping a spare in the climber's kit, but they get expensive for a crew that burns through several gallons a day. The 4.75 gallon size brings the cost per gallon down and cuts the pile of empty cans in the truck.

If you run a lot of fuel, compare the cost with mixing your own using quality oil such as Husqvarna XP 2-stroke oil and ethanol-free gas. Many crews use premix for low-use equipment and seasonal saws and mix their own for daily saws.

Think about how fast you will use it. A bulk container makes the most sense when a crew will go through it in a reasonable time. A homeowner with one saw may be better off buying quarts and opening them as needed.

Keep the container sealed and out of direct sun when it is not in use. Once opened, close it tightly and use it within the period the label recommends. Pour into a clean, labeled fuel can or straight into equipment, outdoors and away from sparks, and let hot saws cool before you refuel.
Before switching a saw from ethanol pump gas to premix, check the carburetor setting with your dealer or the saw's manual. Always follow the engine maker's fuel recommendations.
Keep a small funnel or spout dedicated to premix so it does not pick up dirt or another fluid. Clean fuel matters more in small saw carburetors than most people think.

Any 2-stroke engine that calls for a 50:1 ratio can use it, regardless of brand. Do not use it in 4-stroke engines or in machines that call for a different ratio. When in doubt, check the operator's manual.

At the end of the season, many owners run their saws on premix before storing them. That leaves ethanol-free fuel in the carburetor instead of pump gas that can leave varnish behind, and it makes the first start in spring a lot less frustrating.

faq.q: Can I use Husqvarna premix in other brands of saw?
faq.a: Yes, if the engine is a 2-stroke that calls for a 50:1 mix. Check the operator's manual for the recommended ratio.

faq.q: How long does premixed 2-stroke fuel last?
faq.a: Sealed, it stores much longer than pump gas. Once opened, keep it tightly closed and follow the shelf-life guidance on the label.

faq.q: Do I need to adjust my carburetor for premix?
faq.a: Sometimes. Ethanol-free fuel can run slightly differently than pump gas. Have a dealer check the tune if the saw runs poorly after switching.

name: Husqvarna XP 2-Stroke Synthetic Blend Oil, 12.8 oz Bottle
title: Husqvarna 2 Cycle Oil: XP Synthetic Blend, 12.8 oz
h1: Husqvarna XP 2 Cycle Oil, 12.8 oz Bottle
meta: Husqvarna 2 cycle oil, XP synthetic blend, in a 12.8 oz bottle that mixes 5 gallons of gas at 50:1. How to mix it right and keep saws running clean.
tagline: Synthetic blend 2-stroke mixing oil sized for a 5 gallon can of fuel at 50:1.
summary: This is Husqvarna 2 cycle oil from the XP line, a synthetic blend made for hard-working saws, blowers and trimmers. One 12.8 oz bottle mixes with 5 gallons of gasoline at 50:1, which is the right size for a crew's main fuel can.
highlights: Synthetic blend 2-stroke oil from Husqvarna's XP line
12.8 oz bottle mixes 5 gallons of gas at 50:1
Made for high-revving saws and handheld equipment
Helps keep pistons, rings and exhaust ports cleaner
Works in any 2-stroke engine that calls for 50:1

body.h: Why the oil matters in a saw
p: A 2-stroke saw has no oil sump. Every bit of lubrication for the crankshaft bearings, connecting rod and piston comes from the oil you mix into the fuel. Cheap oil or the wrong ratio shows up as carbon buildup, a scored piston or a saw that will not hold a tune.

Husqvarna XP oil is a synthetic blend made for engines that spend all day at high rpm, which is exactly how a felling saw or a climber's top-handle runs. It is meant to burn clean, protect at high temperature and keep exhaust ports from loading up with carbon.

Top-handle saws in particular run hot and hard. A climber may rev the saw hundreds of times a day for short cuts, with little time at idle to cool. That kind of duty is where a quality synthetic blend earns its price.

At 50:1, one gallon of gas takes about 2.6 fl oz of oil. This 12.8 oz bottle is sized for 5 gallons, so you dump the whole bottle into a clean can, add 5 gallons of fresh gas and shake. No measuring cups, no math on the tailgate.

Put the oil in first, then the gas, so it mixes as you fill. Shake the can before each refuel, since oil can settle if the fuel sits. Use fresh gas at the octane your manual calls for, and use it up within a few weeks. Ethanol fuel goes stale faster than most people think.
If you only need a small batch for a homeowner saw or a climber's spare bottle, the 6.4 oz bottle mixes 2.5 gallons and wastes less.

body.h: Husqvarna mixing oil for the whole crew
p: Using one oil and one ratio for every 2-stroke on the truck takes a lot of risk out of fueling. Saws, pole saws, blowers and trimmers that call for 50:1 all run on the same mix, so nobody has to remember which can goes with which machine. Label the can with the ratio and date you mixed it.

Check each machine's manual before you standardize. Some older equipment calls for a different ratio, and 4-stroke engines never get mixed fuel. If a machine calls for something other than 50:1, keep a separate, clearly marked can for it.
If you would rather skip mixing entirely, Husqvarna 50:1 premix fuel comes ready to pour and stores longer than pump gas.

Keep unopened bottles in a cool, dry place out of the sun. Once you mix fuel, store it in a proper safety can, and do not keep mixed fuel for months. Old fuel is one of the most common reasons saws will not start or idle right.

Refuel with the saw shut off and cooled down, away from where you will start it, and wipe up spills before pulling the cord. Clean fuel, good oil and a sharp chain do more for saw life than almost anything else you can buy.

Keep a log of when each can was mixed, or write the date on a strip of tape on the can. It sounds fussy, but it settles the morning argument about whether the fuel in the back of the truck is still good.

faq.q: How much gas does a 12.8 oz bottle of Husqvarna oil mix?
faq.a: It mixes 5 gallons of gasoline at a 50:1 ratio.

faq.q: Can I use Husqvarna 2 cycle oil in other brands of saws?
faq.a: Yes, in any 2-stroke engine that calls for a 50:1 mix. Check your manual for the recommended ratio and oil type.

faq.q: How long does mixed fuel last?
faq.a: Mixed with regular pump gas, plan to use it within a few weeks. Ethanol-free gas lasts longer. Always shake before use.

faq.q: What happens if I use too little oil?
faq.a: Running lean on oil can overheat and score the piston and cylinder. Stick to the ratio in your manual.

name: Husqvarna XP 2-Stroke Synthetic Blend Oil, 6.4 oz Bottle
title: Husqvarna 2 Cycle Oil: XP Synthetic Blend, 6.4 oz
h1: Husqvarna XP 2 Cycle Oil, 6.4 oz Bottle
meta: Husqvarna 2 cycle oil in a 6.4 oz bottle of XP synthetic blend that mixes 2.5 gallons of gas at 50:1. Right size for one saw, a spare kit or small batches.
tagline: Synthetic blend 2-stroke oil for a 2.5 gallon batch of 50:1 fuel.
summary: The 6.4 oz bottle of Husqvarna 2 cycle oil holds the same XP synthetic blend as the larger size, measured to mix 2.5 gallons of gasoline at 50:1. It suits homeowners, small batches and anyone who wants fresher fuel instead of a big can that sits.
highlights: Husqvarna XP synthetic blend 2-stroke oil
6.4 oz bottle mixes 2.5 gallons at 50:1
Smaller batch means fresher fuel
For saws, trimmers, blowers and pole saws
Easy to stash in a truck box or saw kit

p: The biggest enemy of a saw that only runs now and then is old fuel. Ethanol gas picks up water and goes stale, and a 5 gallon can that takes three months to use is a carburetor problem waiting to happen. The 6.4 oz bottle mixes 2.5 gallons, which is easier to use up while it is still fresh.
It is also the size a lot of people keep as a spare. Toss one in the truck so a crew member can mix a can on site if the main fuel runs out halfway through a removal.

Small bottles also make sense for equipment that needs its own fuel. If you run one older machine that calls for a different ratio, or you want a separate can for the pole saw that only comes out on pruning jobs, a 2.5 gallon batch keeps things simple.

Husqvarna two stroke oil in the XP line is a synthetic blend made for high-rpm handheld engines. In a 2-stroke, the oil in the fuel is the only thing lubricating the bearings and piston, so oil quality has a direct effect on how long the engine lasts and how clean it runs.

A good blend helps keep carbon off the piston crown and out of the muffler screen and exhaust port. That keeps power up and the saw easier to tune. It does not fix a dull chain or a clogged air filter, but it removes one common cause of trouble.

The oil in the fuel also carries heat away from the piston and helps seal the rings. When the oil film breaks down from heat or a lean mix, damage happens quickly. Using a known oil at the correct ratio is cheap protection for an expensive saw.

Pour the full bottle into a clean, labeled fuel can, then add 2.5 gallons of fresh gasoline at the octane your manual calls for. Close the can and shake it. Shake again before every refuel. If you use a different ratio for any machine, keep that mix in its own marked can.
Mixing in the can rather than in the saw tank gives a far more even blend. Never pour oil directly into the saw tank and top it off with gas. That is how pistons get scored.
If your crew burns through fuel quickly, the 12.8 oz bottle mixes a full 5 gallons. For machines that sit for long periods, consider Husqvarna premix fuel, which is ethanol-free and stores better.

Store sealed bottles in a cool, dry spot. Keep mixed fuel in an approved safety can, out of direct sun, and use it within a few weeks if it was made with ethanol pump gas. Refuel with the engine off and cool, away from where you will start it, and clean up spills before starting.
Follow the engine maker's fuel and oil recommendations. If a machine is still under warranty, check what the warranty requires before changing oils.

If you are not sure whether a can of mix is still good, it is cheaper to dispose of it properly and mix a fresh batch than to rebuild a carburetor. Take old fuel to a hazardous waste collection site; do not pour it on the ground.

faq.q: How much gas does a 6.4 oz bottle of Husqvarna oil mix?
faq.a: It mixes 2.5 gallons of gasoline at 50:1.

faq.q: Is Husqvarna XP oil the same as XP+?
faq.a: Husqvarna has sold more than one premium 2-stroke oil under the XP name over the years. Check the label on the bottle you buy for the exact formulation and ratio.

faq.q: Can I use this oil in a 4-stroke engine?
faq.a: No. 2-stroke mixing oil is only for 2-stroke engines that run on mixed fuel.

name: No-Spill Red Fuel Can
title: Red No Spill Gas Can: Push-Button Pour Fuel Can
meta: A red no spill gas can with a thumb-button pour that makes fueling saws, chippers and mowers cleaner. How it works, how to use it and how to store it safely.
tagline: Red push-button fuel can for clean refueling of saws and small engines.
summary: This red No-Spill fuel can is a no spill gas can with a push-button spout that lets you control the flow, so you can fill a saw or a small engine without glugging fuel down the side. It is a simple upgrade over the frustrating spouts on most plastic cans.
highlights: Thumb-button control starts and stops the flow
Red color marks it for gasoline
Easier to pour into small saw tanks without spilling
Durable plastic body for truck and shop use
Good for gas or mixed 2-stroke fuel

body.h: Why a no-spill fuel container helps
p: Most modern plastic cans come with spouts that are hard to start, glug when they flow and dribble when they stop. On a saw, that means fuel down the side of the powerhead, on your gloves and on the ground. A no-spill gas can uses a thumb-operated valve, so the fuel only flows when you press the button and stops the instant you let go.
That control makes the biggest difference with small tanks. Topping off a top-handle saw, a pole saw or a blower on the tailgate is quick and tidy, and you can see the level rise without overfilling.

Less spilled fuel also means less fuel soaking into your chaps or saw pants, where it can break down protective fibers, and less fuel on a hot muffler, where it can flash. Clean refueling is a safety habit, not just a tidiness one.

body.h: Using it on a tree crew
p: Keep one red can for mixed fuel and label it with the ratio, such as 50:1, and the date mixed. Most crews keep a second can for straight gas if they run 4-stroke equipment or a gas chipper. Do not mix them up: straight gas in a 2-stroke saw can ruin the engine in minutes.

Refuel with the engine shut off and cool, on bare ground or the tailgate, away from where you will start the saw. Set the can on a stable surface, put the spout in the tank, then press the button. Release it before you pull the spout out.
Pair it with a metal safety can for bar oil or other fluids so each fluid has its own color and container.

A good habit is to refuel the saw every time you refill bar oil, and to do both at the same spot on the tailgate. Saws should run out of bar oil and fuel at about the same time, and a set routine keeps a climber from running a dry bar aloft.

Keep the cap closed when you are not pouring. Check the spout seal and button for cracks or stickiness now and then, and keep dirt out of the spout so it does not end up in your carburetor. If the button starts to leak, replace the spout or the can.

Plastic cans can swell in the heat. Park the truck in shade when you can and do not leave cans in direct sun all afternoon. Never fill a can while it is sitting in the truck bed; set it on the ground first so static has a path to ground, and fill outdoors away from sparks.
Do not store fuel in the cab or in a closed trailer with ignition sources. Keep cans secured upright in the truck so they cannot tip or roll.

Smaller cans are easier to pour accurately into small saw tanks. Larger cans make sense for fueling a chipper or a fleet of equipment, but get heavy and awkward when full. Many crews carry one small can for saws and a larger can for the bigger engines. Check the listing for the exact capacity before you order.
Whatever size you choose, buy the same style of can for everyone on the crew. When every can works the same way, nobody fumbles a spout they have never used while standing over a hot saw.

faq.q: How does a no spill gas can work?
faq.a: A thumb-operated valve in the spout only lets fuel flow while you hold the button down. Release it and the flow stops.

faq.q: Can I put mixed 2-stroke fuel in a no spill can?
faq.a: Yes. Label the can with the mix ratio so it is never confused with straight gas.

faq.q: Why should I fill a gas can on the ground?
faq.a: Filling a can on the ground gives static a path to dissipate. Filling it in a truck bed liner can let static build up and cause a spark.

name: Hardhead Felling Wedge
title: Hardhead Felling Wedge: Plastic Wedge for Felling & Bucking
meta: A Hardhead felling wedge for lifting a tree through the cut and keeping the bar free when bucking. How to pick a size, stack wedges and drive them safely.
tagline: Plastic felling and bucking wedge that is safe to hit with an axe and safe near a chain.
summary: The Hardhead felling wedge is a durable plastic wedge built to be driven behind the saw to lift a tree toward its lay and to keep the bar from getting pinched when bucking. Plastic wedges will not wreck a chain if the saw touches them, which is why every saw kit should carry a few.
highlights: Tough plastic body that will not ruin a chain on contact
Textured faces help it grip instead of popping out
Use for felling lift and to stop bar pinch while bucking
Stacks with other wedges for extra lift
Fits easily in a wedge pouch or logging belt

p: Every tree has some lean, and few lean exactly where you want them to go. A felling wedge goes into the back cut behind the bar and, as you drive it, lifts the tree off the stump and tips it toward the face. It also keeps the kerf open so the tree cannot sit back on your bar.

When bucking, a wedge in the top of the cut stops the log from closing on the bar. If you have ever spent ten minutes freeing a pinched saw with a second saw and a lot of words, you know why it pays to set a wedge early.

Wedges also help on trees that are close to balanced. A few taps can tip a tree that wants to sit on the stump, and a set wedge keeps the cut from closing if a gust pushes the top the wrong way while you finish the back cut.

Plastic wedges are designed to be cut by mistake. If the chain touches a plastic wedge, you lose a little plastic and maybe some sharpness. If it touches a steel wedge, you lose the chain and possibly more. That is why plastic and composite wedges are standard for saw work, while steel wedges are kept for splitting firewood.
A hard head on the wedge resists mushrooming when it is struck, so it lasts longer and drives more predictably. Keep the striking end square and replace wedges that have split or worn into a dome.

Some plastics get brittle in cold weather. In winter, strike the wedge squarely and check it for cracks more often. A cracked wedge can split under a blow and drop out of the cut just when you need it.

Plan the felling cut before you start: escape route, hinge size and where the wedge will go. Set the wedge as soon as the back cut is deep enough to take it, while the bar is still in the cut. Drive it with the back of an axe or a dedicated hammer, not with the saw.

Watch the top of the tree as you drive. If the tree is not lifting, stop and reassess rather than cutting more hinge. Stacking two wedges gives more lift, but heavy back-leaners may need a pull line or mechanical help instead. Felling is skilled work; get trained before you take down trees, and follow ANSI Z133 and your company's procedures.
Carry wedges where you can reach them, such as a logging belt with a wedge pouch.

Keep the bar running and parallel to the wedge as you drive it, and never stand directly behind a tree that is moving. When the tree starts to go, leave the wedge, take your saw and move out along your escape route.

Short wedges suit smaller trees and bucking; longer, taller wedges give more lift for bigger diameter trees. Most sawyers carry two or three sizes. Check the listing for the size, and match it to your bar length so the wedge fits the cut without hitting the chain.
Write your initials or crew name on your wedges. They get left at stumps and buried in chips, and marked wedges have a better chance of finding their way back to the right truck.

faq.q: Can I hit a plastic felling wedge with a steel axe?
faq.a: Yes. Use the poll of an axe or a hammer designed for driving wedges. Strike squarely to avoid glancing blows.

faq.q: How many wedges should I carry?
faq.a: Most sawyers carry at least two, often in two sizes, so they can stack for more lift or use one while bucking.

faq.q: When should I replace a wedge?
faq.a: Retire wedges that are split, cracked or so mushroomed that they no longer drive straight.

name: Logging Belt Kit
title: Logging Belt Kit: Wedge Pouch, Tape and Tool Holder
meta: A logging belt kit that keeps wedges, a loggers tape and saw tools on your hip. How sawyers set up a loggers belt for felling, bucking and timber work.
tagline: Belt and pouches that keep wedges, tape and saw tools within reach.
summary: A logging belt keeps the gear you reach for every few minutes on your hip instead of back at the truck. This kit pairs a work belt with pouches for wedges and a tape holder, so felling and bucking go faster.
highlights: Belt with pouches for wedges and small tools
Holds a loggers tape where you can reach it
Keeps the scrench and file handy
Frees your hands for the saw

body.h: How sawyers set up a loggers belt
p: Most sawyers set the wedge pouch on the side opposite their saw hand, with a loggers tape clipped at the back or hip where it pays out cleanly. A file and a bar wrench ride in a small pocket, so a chain can be touched up or tensioned without walking back to the truck.
Keep the load light enough that you can move freely. A couple of felling wedges, a tape, a file and a wrench cover most days. Add an axe or a small hammer only if you drive wedges often.
A good loggers belt also saves your knees and back. Every trip to the truck for a forgotten wedge is another walk across rough ground with a hot saw. Keep the tools on you and the work goes faster.
Keep the tape on the same side as your measuring hand and practice pulling and hooking it. A tape that pays out smoothly from the belt makes bucking to length faster and more accurate.

Wear the belt snug at the hips so it does not slide around when you bend to buck. Check stitching and buckles from time to time and replace worn parts before they let go. A logging belt is a tool carrier, not life-support gear: never clip into it to climb or position. Climbing requires a proper arborist saddle that meets the applicable standard.
Wash off sap and mud at the end of the week and let the belt dry fully before storing it. Wet leather and webbing wear faster and can rot if left balled up in the truck.

faq.q: Is a logging belt the same as an arborist belt?
faq.a: No. A logging belt only carries tools. An arborist climbing saddle is life-support equipment that must meet the applicable standard.

faq.q: What should I carry on a logging belt?
faq.a: Usually two or more wedges, a loggers tape, a chain file and a bar wrench.

name: Chainsaw Bar Wrench
title: Chainsaw Wrench: Bar Nut Wrench and Screwdriver Tool
meta: A chainsaw wrench with a bar nut socket and screwdriver tip for tensioning chain, swapping bars and adjusting the carb. Check size and fit before you order.
tagline: The bar wrench, or scrench, every saw kit should have: bar nuts, tension and carb tweaks.
summary: A chainsaw wrench, often called a scrench, combines a bar nut socket with a flat screwdriver tip on one simple tool. It is what you reach for to tension a chain, swap a bar or make a quick idle adjustment on the job.
highlights: Socket for bar nuts plus screwdriver tip
Tension chain and change bars in the field
Small enough for a pocket or logging belt
Cheap insurance against losing the one that came with the saw
Keep one in every saw case
specs: Chain tension, bar changes, minor adjustments
Check socket size against your saw's bar nuts

body.h: The chainsaw tool you use the most
p: A chain stretches as it warms up and wears, and a loose chain can jump the bar. Tensioning it is a two-minute job if you have a wrench in your pocket and a ten-minute walk if the only one is in the truck. That is why sawyers keep a chainsaw wrench on the belt, in the saw case and in the truck box.

The screwdriver end handles the chain tensioner screw on most saws, plus quick idle adjustments and loosening the screws on air filter covers. The socket end fits the bar nuts. Together they cover almost everything you do to a saw in the field besides sharpening.

It also comes in handy for quick checks that prevent bigger problems: snugging a loose handle screw, opening the clutch cover to clear packed chips, or tightening a muffler bolt that has backed out. Small fixes done early keep a saw running all season.

Bar nut sizes vary by brand and model. Before ordering, check the socket size the saw's manual lists, or measure the nut. A wrench that fits loosely rounds the nuts over time and slips when you need to break them free.
If you run saws from more than one brand, keep a wrench that fits each, and label them. Crews that run mixed fleets often lose time hunting for the right one.

Some saws use captive bar nuts or tool-less tensioning systems. Even then, a wrench comes in handy for the occasional stubborn nut or for adjusting the carburetor, so it is still worth keeping one in the kit.

With the saw off and the chain brake on, loosen the bar nuts slightly. Lift the nose of the bar and turn the tensioner until the chain sits snug against the bottom of the bar but can still be pulled around by hand with gloves on. Holding the nose up, tighten the bar nuts firmly.

Recheck tension after the first few cuts with a new chain and whenever the chain has cooled after a long run, since a chain tensioned hot can tighten too much as it cools. Wear gloves when handling the chain.
Pair the wrench with a good file kit from our wrenches and files section to keep the saw cutting well all day.

A chain that is too tight wastes power, overheats the bar and wears the sprocket. A chain that is too loose can derail and is more likely to cause damage or injury. Check tension at every refuel and you will rarely have either problem.

Bar wrenches are easy to lose in leaves and chips. Painting the handle a bright color helps, and a cheap spare in the glovebox has saved more than one job. Replace any wrench whose socket is cracked or worn round.

faq.q: What is a scrench?
faq.a: It is a combination tool with a bar nut socket on one end and a screwdriver tip on the other, used to tension chains and change bars.

faq.q: Will this chainsaw wrench fit my saw?
faq.a: Check the bar nut size in your saw's manual or measure the nut, and compare it with the socket size in the listing.

faq.q: How tight should a chainsaw chain be?
faq.a: Snug against the bottom of the bar but still easy to pull around by hand with gloves on. Always check with the saw off and the brake on.

name: Chipper Knife, 7.25 x 4 x 3/8 in
title: Chipper Knife 7.25 x 4 x 3/8 in: Fit and Sharpening
meta: A 7.25 x 4 x 3/8 in chipper knife for brush chippers. How to confirm fit, when to sharpen or flip, and how to swap knives safely with the machine locked out.
tagline: Replacement brush chipper knife measuring 7.25 x 4 x 3/8 inches.
summary: This replacement chipper knife measures 7.25 x 4 x 3/8 inches and fits brush chippers built around that blade size. Sharp knives feed better, burn less fuel and throw chips farther, so keep a spare set on hand.
highlights: Measures 7.25 in long, 4 in wide, 3/8 in thick
Replacement for brush chippers that use this knife size
Can be resharpened to extend its life
Keep a spare set to swap in on site
Confirm bolt pattern and bevel before ordering
specs: Match size, bolt holes and bevel to your machine

p: Chipper knives are sold by size, but the size alone does not guarantee a fit. Before ordering a 7.25 x 4 knife, measure your old knife for length, width and thickness, then check the number, size and spacing of the bolt holes and the bevel angle. Compare those with the listing and with your chipper's parts manual.

If your knife has been sharpened many times, it may be narrower than new. Measure the widest unworn edge or check the parts book for the original dimension. When in doubt, contact the chipper maker or a dealer with your model and serial number.
Write down the dimensions of the knives your chipper takes and keep them with the machine's records. When you need a set in a hurry, you will not have to pull a knife just to measure it.

Dull knives show up fast on the job. The chipper stops self-feeding, brush has to be pushed in, the engine bogs, and chips come out stringy instead of clean. You also burn more fuel and put more strain on bearings and belts.

Inspect knives at a regular interval in the hours your manual recommends, and right after any hit on a rock, nail or piece of steel. Chips, cracks or a rolled edge mean the knife needs to be sharpened or replaced. Check the anvil, or bed knife, at the same time. A worn anvil makes even sharp knives cut poorly.

Feeding practices make a big difference to knife life. Shake dirt and rocks out of brush before it goes in, keep the infeed area clear of gravel, and watch for wire, nails and old fence in yard trees. A single hidden staple can chip a fresh edge.

Chipper drums and discs carry a lot of stored energy. Before any knife work, shut the engine off, remove the key, wait for the rotor to stop completely, and lock the rotor per the manufacturer's procedure. Follow your company's lockout steps and the chipper manual. Never reach into the infeed or housing with the rotor turning.

Wear cut-resistant gloves when handling knives. Clean the seat and bolts, replace bolts that are stretched or damaged, and torque them to the value in the manual. Knives are often changed in matched sets so the rotor stays balanced.

Many knives can be resharpened several times by a shop that grinds chipper knives, keeping the original bevel and removing metal evenly across a set. Keep one sharp set in the truck and one at the shop, and you can swap and send out for sharpening without losing a day. Browse other chipper knives if your machine takes a different size.

Track hours between sharpenings for each set. If knives start dulling much faster than usual, check your feeding practices, the anvil gap and whether you are chipping a lot of dirty or sandy material.

faq.q: Will a 7.25 x 4 knife fit my chipper?
faq.a: Only if the length, width, thickness, bolt pattern and bevel match. Measure your existing knife and check your chipper's parts manual.

faq.q: How often should chipper knives be sharpened?
faq.a: Follow your chipper manual's interval and inspect after any hit on rock or metal. Feeding problems and stringy chips are signs they are dull.

faq.q: Should I replace chipper knives in sets?
faq.a: It is a good practice, since matched knives keep the rotor balanced and cut evenly.

name: Chipper Knife for Vermeer BC1800XL
title: Vermeer BC1800XL Chipper Knife: Replacement Blade
meta: Replacement chipper knife for the Vermeer BC1800XL drum chipper. How to confirm fit, spot dull knives and swap a set safely with the rotor locked out.
tagline: Aftermarket replacement knife for the Vermeer BC1800XL brush chipper.
summary: This is a replacement knife for the Vermeer BC1800XL, one of the most common large drum chippers on tree crews. Sharp knives keep the machine self-feeding and save fuel, belts and bearings.
highlights: Replacement knife for the Vermeer BC1800XL
Can be resharpened to extend service life
Change in matched sets to keep the drum balanced
Keep a spare set to swap on the job
specs: Vermeer BC1800XL (confirm with your parts manual)

p: Vermeer has built the BC1800 family over many years and updated parts along the way, so confirm the knife against your chipper's parts manual and serial number before ordering. Measure your old knife and compare the bolt pattern and bevel.

Change or sharpen knives when brush stops pulling in on its own, the engine bogs on material it used to eat, or chips come out stringy. Check the anvil at the same time. A worn anvil gap makes sharp knives cut poorly. See other chipper knives if you run more than one machine.

Knife life depends heavily on what goes through the machine. Brush dragged across gravel, roadside trees with embedded wire and dirty storm debris all dull knives faster. Shake out root balls and keep the infeed area clean, and a set will go much longer between sharpenings.

Shut the engine off, pull the key, wait for the drum to stop completely and lock the drum as the manual describes before you open the housing. Follow your company's lockout procedure. Wear cut-resistant gloves, clean the knife seats, replace damaged bolts and torque them to the manual value. Never reach into the infeed or housing while anything is turning.

Knives are usually changed or rotated as a set so the drum stays balanced. If one knife is chipped badly, replace or grind the whole set to match. Keep a sharp spare set in the shop so swapping does not cost a day of production.

faq.q: Is this knife made by Vermeer?
faq.a: It is an aftermarket replacement built to fit the BC1800XL. Check dimensions and your parts manual before ordering.

faq.q: How many knives does a BC1800XL use?
faq.a: Check your operator's or parts manual for the knife count and part numbers for your serial number range, and order a full set.

name: Chipper Knife for Vermeer BC2100
title: Vermeer Chipper Blades for the BC2100 Drum Chipper
h1: Vermeer Chipper Blades for the BC2100
meta: Replacement Vermeer chipper blades for the BC2100 drum chipper. Confirm fit, know when knives need sharpening and change them safely with the drum locked.
tagline: Aftermarket replacement knife for the Vermeer BC2100 whole-tree chipper.
summary: These replacement Vermeer chipper blades are made for the BC2100, a big drum chipper built for large wood and whole-tree work. Sharp knives keep a machine that size feeding hard and running efficiently.
highlights: Replacement knife for the Vermeer BC2100
Resharpenable for longer service
Order a full matched set for balance
Keep spares to avoid downtime
specs: Vermeer BC2100 (confirm with your parts manual)

p: Vermeer chipper knives are model-specific. A knife for a BC1250 or BC1800 will not necessarily fit a BC2100, so check your parts manual and serial number, measure your old knife and compare the bolt pattern and bevel with the listing. When in doubt, ask your dealer for the original part number and cross-reference it.

Big chippers chew through a lot of wood. Watch for slower feeding, the engine pulling down on wood it used to take easily, and rough chips. Inspect the anvil gap whenever you service knives. A worn anvil makes sharp knives work harder.

Large chippers are also hard on knives because of the size of wood they take. Big, dense hardwood and frozen wood in winter both wear edges faster. Keep a record of hours between sharpenings so you can spot when something is off, such as a wrong anvil gap or a lot of dirty material.

A large drum carries a lot of momentum. Shut down, remove the key, wait for the drum to stop and lock it in place per the manual before opening anything. Follow lockout procedures, wear cut-resistant gloves, use new bolts where the manual calls for them and torque to spec. Keep a sharp set at the shop so you can swap and send the dull set out for grinding. Other sizes are in our chipper knives section.
After installing a new or sharpened set, run the machine empty for a moment and listen for vibration or contact before feeding wood. Any unusual noise means shut down, lock out and recheck.

faq.q: Do these Vermeer wood chipper blades fit other models?
faq.a: Knives are specific to the machine. Confirm the part against your model and serial number before ordering.

faq.q: Can Vermeer chipper knives be sharpened?
faq.a: Yes. A shop that grinds chipper knives can resharpen them several times while keeping the correct bevel.

name: Grounds Keeper Rake, Complete
title: Grounds Keeper Rake: Scrape Rake for Tree Job Cleanup
meta: The Grounds Keeper rake is a scrape rake with stiff spring tines that pulls chips, twigs and sawdust out of turf. Why tree crews keep one on every truck.
tagline: Stiff-tined scrape rake that cleans chips and twigs out of lawns after tree work.
summary: The Grounds Keeper is a scrape rake built for cleanup: its stiff, closely spaced tines pull wood chips, sawdust, twigs and leaves out of turf in a way a leaf rake cannot. Tree crews use it to leave a yard cleaner than they found it.
highlights: Stiff spring tines that scrape debris out of grass
Handles chips, sawdust, twigs and gravel spill
Replaceable tines and handle extend its life
Tough enough for daily crew use
A favorite final-cleanup tool on removals
specs: Cleanup of chips, sawdust, twigs, leaves

body.h: Why tree crews love this rake
p: The last half hour of a removal decides what the customer remembers. Sawdust piles under the bucking area, chips blown out of the chipper chute and small twigs stuck in the grass all make a yard look worked over. A leaf rake rides over the top of that mess. A scrape rake digs in.

The Grounds Keeper uses stiff spring tines set close together. They comb down into the thatch, flick out chips and twigs, and pull everything into a pile without tearing up healthy turf when used with a light hand. Crews that try one usually end up buying one for every truck.

It is not just for lawns. Crews use it to pull chips out of mulch beds, rake sawdust off patios before blowing, and clean up the small stuff around a stump after grinding. Anything small and annoying that a leaf rake leaves behind, this rake tends to catch.

body.h: How to get the best results
p: Work in short pulls toward a tarp or the pile, rather than long sweeping strokes. Let the tines do the work. Pressing down hard tears grass and wears tines faster. On sawdust, rake first, then finish with a blower such as the Husqvarna 125B to clear what is left on driveways and beds.

It also works well on gravel driveways where chips land, for pulling debris out of shrub beds and for spreading mulch. On hard surfaces, use a lighter touch to avoid scraping the tines across concrete.

Lay a tarp down before you start and rake onto it. A tarp drags easily to the chipper or the truck and saves a lot of bending over with a pitchfork. For big jobs, two people raking toward the same tarp clears a yard fast.

Rakes take a beating on a tree crew. Handles snap when someone uses them as a pry bar, and tines get bent on roots and curbs. The Grounds Keeper is designed so you can replace parts rather than the whole tool. Replacement tines and a replacement handle are sold separately, so one rake head can last for years.
Check the tines regularly. Bent tines can often be straightened by hand, but cracked or broken tines should be swapped so the rake keeps cleaning evenly.
Buying wear parts instead of whole tools also cuts down on what ends up in the dumpster at the end of the season, and it means every rake on the truck works the same way.

Store the rake on a rack or in a tube on the truck where it will not get run over or bent under logs. Knock off sap and mud at the end of the day and check that the head is still tight on the handle. A loose head wastes effort with every pull.
Wear gloves when raking cleanup debris. Splinters, thorns and hidden glass are common in yards, and gloves make long cleanup sessions easier on your hands.
At the end of the season, check the tine fasteners and the handle joint and replace anything worn before spring. Starting the busy season with a tight, straight rake saves time on every job.

faq.q: What is a scrape rake?
faq.a: A rake with stiff, closely spaced tines that digs into grass and pulls out small debris like chips, sawdust and twigs.

faq.q: Will a Grounds Keeper rake damage my lawn?
faq.a: Used with light, short strokes it removes debris without much damage. Heavy pressure can tear grass.

faq.q: Can I replace the tines and handle?
faq.a: Yes. Replacement tines and handles are sold separately so you can rebuild the rake instead of replacing it.

name: Grounds Keeper Rake Replacement Handle
title: Rake Handle Replacement for the Grounds Keeper Rake
meta: A rake handle replacement for the Grounds Keeper scrape rake. Get a broken rake back to work fast, with tips on swapping the handle and making it last.
tagline: Replacement handle that puts a broken Grounds Keeper rake back in service.
summary: This is a rake handle replacement for the Grounds Keeper scrape rake, so a snapped or cracked handle does not mean buying a whole new tool. Swap the handle, keep the head and the rake is back on the truck.
highlights: Made for the Grounds Keeper rake head
Cheaper than buying a complete rake
Keeps a favorite rake in service for years
Good spare to keep at the shop
Simple to install
specs: Replacing a broken or cracked handle
Handle only; head and tines sold separately

body.h: Why handles break on tree crews
p: Rakes on a tree crew live hard lives. Someone uses one to lever a round off the trailer, another gets left under a log on the ground, and a third gets backed over in the driveway. Most of the time the head is fine and only the handle is done.
Replacing the handle costs a fraction of a new rake and keeps a head you have already worn in. That is the main reason the Grounds Keeper design is popular: wear parts are sold on their own.

Rebuilding also keeps the rake's feel consistent. A head whose tines are already set the way you like them rakes better than a brand-new one, so many crew leaders would rather swap a handle than buy a new rake.

Remove the old handle from the head, following the fastening method used on your rake. Clean out any splinters or dirt from the socket, seat the new handle fully and refasten it so the head does not wobble. Check it again after the first day of use, since a new fit can settle a little.
If your tines are bent or broken while you have the rake apart, this is a good time to fit replacement tines as well. A rebuilt rake with a fresh handle and tines works like a new one.

Confirm that the handle matches your rake before ordering. Grounds Keeper has offered more than one rake model over time, and handles for other brands of rakes are often a different size or attachment style.

A rake is for raking. Use a pry bar, a cant hook or a hookaroon to move wood instead of the rake handle, and you will replace far fewer of them. Store rakes on a rack or in a tube on the truck, not loose in the bed where logs and gear get thrown on top.

If a handle has a crack, replace it before it fails mid-pull. A snapped handle can leave a sharp, splintered end that is easy to get hurt on. Wear gloves when handling a broken handle and when cleaning up debris.
Wipe handles down at the end of the day and keep them out of standing water when the truck is parked. Sap and grime make them slippery and harder to grip, especially in the rain.
A rake that is dragged across asphalt or concrete at the end of the day also takes wear at the head and the handle joint. Carry it to the truck instead of dragging it behind you.

body.h: Keep a spare at the shop
p: Crews that run several trucks often keep one or two spare handles at the shop so a broken rake can be fixed the same evening. It is a cheap way to make sure every truck goes out in the morning with a working cleanup rake, and it keeps the customer's yard looking right at the end of every job.

faq.q: Will this handle fit other rakes?
faq.a: It is made for the Grounds Keeper rake head. Other brands often use different sockets, so check fit before ordering.

faq.q: Does it come with tines or a head?
faq.a: No, it is the handle only. Replacement tines and complete rakes are sold separately.

faq.q: How do I keep a rake handle from breaking?
faq.a: Use it only for raking, store it where it will not get crushed, and replace cracked handles before they fail.

name: Grounds Keeper Rake Replacement Tines
title: Replacement Rake Tines for the Grounds Keeper Rake
meta: Replacement rake tines for the Grounds Keeper scrape rake. Swap bent or broken spring tines and your cleanup rake pulls chips and twigs from turf like new.
tagline: Spring steel replacement tines that restore a worn Grounds Keeper rake.
summary: These replacement rake tines are made for the Grounds Keeper scrape rake. When tines bend, break or wear short, swapping them brings back the stiff, even scraping action that makes the rake so good at pulling chips and twigs out of grass.
highlights: Spring steel tines for the Grounds Keeper rake
Restore even contact across the full rake head
Cheaper than replacing the whole rake
Good to keep on hand for busy cleanup seasons
Pair with a new handle for a full rebuild

p: Spring tines take a lot of punishment: roots, curbs, rocks and the occasional sprinkler head. Over time some bend out of line, some snap and the rest wear short from scraping. A rake with uneven tines leaves stripes of debris behind and makes you go over the same area twice.
If more than a couple of tines are bent beyond easy straightening, or any are broken, it is time to replace them. A fresh set restores the stiff, even comb that makes a scrape rake worth carrying.

Worn tines also leave the rake head sitting at a different angle to the ground, which changes how it feels in your hands and makes you push harder. Fresh tines bring the rake back to its intended working angle.

Wear gloves, since spring steel tines can snap back when they are being seated. Remove the old tines following the fastening method on your rake head, clean out dirt and debris, then fit the new tines so they sit evenly and point the same direction. Tighten everything and check that none of the tines move side to side.

Make sure the tines are for your rake. These are made for the Grounds Keeper. Landscape rakes, rock rakes and york rakes use different tines and attachment methods, so parts usually do not swap between brands.
If the handle is cracked or loose while the rake is apart, add a replacement handle and the whole tool is effectively new.
Replace tines in a full set where you can. Mixing old and new tines leaves some longer than others, and the short ones never touch the ground.

body.h: Getting more life from your tines
p: Rake with short, light strokes and let the tines do the work. Bearing down hard bends tines and tears turf. On gravel and hard surfaces, lift the rake slightly so the tips skim rather than dig.
Do not use the rake to drag heavy branches or pry at roots. Grab a pitchfork or a hookaroon for that. Store the rake head up or on a rack so the tines are not crushed under logs or gear in the truck.
Clean the head at the end of the day. Packed mud and sap between tines hold moisture and encourage rust, and a clean head rakes more freely the next morning.

Cleanup is the last thing the customer sees on a tree job. A rake that leaves sawdust and twigs in the grass undoes a lot of good work. Keeping a set of spare tines at the shop means a worn rake can be fixed the same day.
If you do not own a Grounds Keeper yet, the complete rake comes ready to use.
Tines are a wear item, much like chainsaw chain or chipper knives. Budget for them the same way, and they will never catch you without a working rake.

faq.q: Will these tines fit a landscape or york rake?
faq.a: No. They are made for the Grounds Keeper rake. Other rakes use different tines and attachment methods.

faq.q: Can I straighten bent rake tines?
faq.a: Slightly bent tines can often be bent back by hand with gloves on. Replace tines that are cracked, broken or badly kinked.

faq.q: How many tines are in a set?
faq.a: Check the listing for the tine count and confirm it matches what your rake head holds.

name: Hasegawa Orchard Ladder
title: Hasegawa Orchard Ladder: Tripod Ladder for Pruning
meta: The Hasegawa orchard ladder is a Japanese aluminum tripod ladder for pruning hedges, small trees and fruit trees. How to pick a height and set it up safely.
tagline: Japanese aluminum tripod ladder for pruning, hedges and orchard work.
summary: The Hasegawa orchard ladder is a Japanese tripod ladder made from aluminum, with two climbing legs and a single adjustable rear leg. That third leg lets it stand steady on slopes, soft ground and in planting beds where a regular stepladder rocks.
highlights: Tripod design stands on uneven and soft ground
Lightweight aluminum construction
Adjustable rear leg for slopes and beds
Narrow top fits into hedges and tree canopies
Available in several heights

body.h: Why a tripod ladder for pruning
p: A stepladder needs a flat, firm surface, and most pruning happens on lawns, mulch beds and slopes. A tripod orchard ladder puts its single rear leg into the middle of a bed or uphill on a slope, and its wide-splayed front legs stay planted on soft ground. The narrow top lets you get into a hedge or close to a trunk where a stepladder's wide top would not fit.

Hasegawa is a Japanese maker known for these ladders, and their design is a favorite with gardeners, hedge crews and arborists who do a lot of small-tree pruning and fruit tree work. They are light enough to carry with one hand between trees.

They also shine on hedge work. A long hedge on a slope or along a planting bed is slow and risky to cut from a stepladder that keeps shifting. With a tripod ladder, the rear leg goes into the bed and the front legs stand on the lawn, and you can work along the hedge in steady steps.

Pick a height that lets you reach the work while standing at or below the highest step the manufacturer allows, with your hips inside the rails. Do not stand on the top. If you regularly reach for cuts above your shoulders, choose a taller ladder or use a pole saw or pole pruner from the ground instead.
Taller tripod ladders are more stable at their base but heavier to carry and harder to fit between plants. Many hedge and orchard crews keep two sizes so they always have the right one for the job.

Height is usually measured to the top of the ladder, not to the highest standing step. Check the listing for both figures, and remember your comfortable reach is roughly your height plus a little above your head, not the length of a pole tool.

Spread the front legs fully and lock any spreaders. Set the rear leg so the ladder stands upright and the rear foot is on firm ground, not on a loose stone or root. On slopes, place the rear leg uphill when possible. Push down on the ladder before climbing to make sure all three feet have settled.

Keep three points of contact while climbing, face the ladder, and do not overreach. Move the ladder rather than leaning out. Check the load rating on the label and include the weight of your tools. Do not use an aluminum ladder near power lines. Keep at least the minimum approach distance required for your qualification under ANSI Z133 and OSHA, and treat every line as energized.

Before each use, check for bent rails, cracked welds or rivets, loose steps and worn feet. Remove a damaged ladder from service and tag it. Rinse off sap and dirt, store it out of the weather when you can, and secure it well on the truck so it does not get bent under logs or gear. Pair it with good landscaper tools and a sharp hand saw for efficient small-tree work.
Retire a ladder that has been in a fall or a strong impact, even if damage is not obvious. Aluminum can crack at joints in ways that are hard to see.

faq.q: What is an orchard ladder?
faq.a: A three-legged ladder with two front legs and one rear leg, designed to stand steady on soft or uneven ground for pruning and harvesting.

faq.q: Can I use a Hasegawa ladder on a slope?
faq.a: Yes, the adjustable rear leg is designed for uneven ground. Set it so the ladder stands upright and all three feet are firmly planted.

faq.q: Is an orchard ladder a substitute for climbing a tree?
faq.a: No. It is for work you can reach safely from the ladder. Higher work calls for a pole tool, an aerial lift or a trained climber.

name: Husqvarna 27 in Universal Axe
title: Husqvarna Axes: 27 in Universal Axe for Field Work
meta: The 27 in universal axe is one of the most useful Husqvarna axes for tree crews: limbing, driving wedges and light splitting. Uses, care and safe handling.
tagline: All-round wooden-handled axe for limbing, driving wedges and light splitting.
summary: Among Husqvarna axes, the 27 in universal axe is the all-rounder: long enough for real swings, light enough to carry all day. It handles limbing, driving wedges and splitting kindling on the job site.
highlights: 27 in handle for a full two-handed swing
Forged steel head
Wooden handle that absorbs shock
Poll can drive plastic felling wedges
Leather edge cover for transport

p: A universal axe sits between a small hatchet and a splitting maul. On a tree job it knocks small limbs off a log, drives felling wedges with the poll and splits a round when the saw is not the right tool. At home it handles firewood and camp chores.

For heavy splitting, a dedicated splitting axe or maul does the job with less effort. For carrying on a belt all day, a smaller hatchet is lighter. If you only want one axe on the truck, a 27 in universal is a sensible choice.
A universal axe is also handy around the chipper. It trims off crotches and forks that will not feed, and it can split a wide piece of trunk wood that is too big to go through the throat.

Keep the edge sharp with a file or stone. A dull axe glances off wood, which is when injuries happen. Check that the head is tight on the handle before every use, and retire the handle if it cracks. Keep the edge cover on when it is not in use.
Clear your swing path, keep bystanders well back and stand so a missed swing goes into the ground, not your leg. Wear eye protection and sturdy boots.
Oil a wooden handle with boiled linseed oil once or twice a season to keep it from drying out and cracking.

faq.q: Can I drive wedges with a Husqvarna axe?
faq.a: Plastic felling wedges, yes, with the poll. Do not strike steel wedges with an axe poll unless the manufacturer says it is designed for that.

faq.q: How do I sharpen a Husqvarna axe?
faq.a: Use a file or a sharpening stone, keeping the original bevel angle, and finish with a fine stone.

name: Husqvarna 31 in Splitting Axe
title: Husqvarna Splitting Axe, 31 in: Firewood and Rounds
meta: The Husqvarna splitting axe with a 31 in handle and wedge-shaped head for splitting rounds into firewood. How to use it safely and keep it in good shape.
tagline: Long-handled splitting axe with a wedge head for breaking rounds into firewood.
summary: This Husqvarna splitting axe pairs a long 31 in handle with a wedge-shaped head that drives into a round and forces it apart. It is the tool for turning a pile of rounds from a removal into firewood.
highlights: 31 in handle for a full, powerful swing
Wedge-shaped head that splits rather than cuts
Forged steel head
Wooden handle
Edge cover included for storage and transport

p: A universal axe has a thinner head that bites into wood. A splitting axe has a thicker, wedge-shaped head that drives in and pushes the fibers apart. That makes it far better at breaking rounds, and the long handle gives more speed at the head for less effort.
If you mostly limb and drive wedges, the Husqvarna 27 in universal axe is the better fit. If you split a lot of firewood from removals, get the splitting axe.
Remember that a long handle means a wide swing arc. Give yourself more room than you think you need, and check above for low branches before you start.

Split on a solid chopping block, not on the ground, so a miss goes into the block. Read the round and aim for existing cracks. Keep your feet apart and let the head fall through the swing. Keep bystanders well back, wear eye protection and boots, and check the head is tight before each session. Keep the edge reasonably sharp and replace a cracked handle right away.

Wipe the head after use and keep a light coat of oil on it to prevent rust, and oil the wooden handle occasionally so it does not dry out and crack. Store it with the edge cover on, away from where people reach into the truck.

faq.q: Is a splitting axe the same as a maul?
faq.a: A maul is heavier and blunter, used for big or knotty rounds. A splitting axe is lighter and faster for most firewood.

faq.q: Can I chop trees with a splitting axe?
faq.a: It is not designed for felling or limbing. Use a universal or felling axe for cutting across the grain.

name: Husqvarna A2400 Multi-Purpose Axe, Fiber Handle
title: Husqvarna Axe A2400: Multi-Purpose Fiber Handle Axe
meta: The Husqvarna axe A2400 is a multi-purpose axe with a tough composite handle for limbing, light splitting and chores. Who it suits and how to care for it.
tagline: Composite-handled multi-purpose axe for limbing, splitting and general chores.
summary: The A2400 is a Husqvarna axe with a fiber composite handle, built as a multi-purpose tool for limbing, light splitting and the general chopping that comes up on tree jobs and at home. The composite handle shrugs off weather and abuse that would ruin a wooden one.
highlights: Composite fiber handle that resists weather and rot
Multi-purpose head for limbing and light splitting
Low-maintenance choice for the truck
Balanced for one- or two-handed use
Comes with an edge guard

p: Wooden handles feel great but need care. Left in a wet truck bed they swell, dry out, crack and work loose. A composite handle does not care if it rides in the rain all week. It is also more forgiving of an overstrike, where the handle rather than the head hits the wood, which is the classic way wooden handles break.
That makes the A2400 a good truck axe for crews that are hard on tools, and for anyone who wants an axe that is ready when they need it without oiling the handle every season.

Composite handles also tend to be lighter for their length than hickory, so the axe moves fast. That said, some people prefer the feel and feedback of wood. If you already own a good wooden-handled axe you like, this makes a solid second axe for the truck or the trailer.

On a tree job, the multi purpose axe knocks off small limbs, notches a stump for a grinder, trims roots, splits a few rounds, and drives plastic felling wedges with the poll. At home it splits kindling and handles camp chores.

It is a compromise tool. For serious firewood splitting, a Husqvarna splitting axe does the job faster. For clean limbing on big logs, a saw is usually faster still. But as one axe that does a bit of everything, it earns its spot on the truck.
It is also a good choice for the ground person who wants one axe on the trailer that nobody needs to baby. When it gets left out overnight in the rain, it is fine the next morning.

Before swinging, check that the head is tight, the edge is sound and there is nothing in your swing path, including overhead branches. Keep other people well back. Stand so that if the axe glances or misses, it goes into the ground or the block, not into your leg or foot. Wear eye protection, gloves and sturdy boots.

Limb from the opposite side of the log where possible, so the log is between you and the edge. Do not chop near rocks or dirt; they ruin the edge and can make the head bounce. When you are tired, stop. Most axe injuries happen late in the day.
