Keep the edge sharp with a file or stone, holding the original bevel. A sharp axe bites; a dull axe glances. Wipe the head after use and keep a light coat of oil on it to prevent rust, especially if it rides in a damp truck. Keep the edge guard on in transport and storage. Inspect the handle regularly and replace the axe if the handle or head cracks.

Use a guide or a puck-style stone for sharpening in the field, and save heavy reshaping for the bench with a file and vise. Never use a bench grinder at high speed without cooling the steel, since overheating can ruin the temper of the edge.

faq.q: Is a composite handle better than wood?
faq.a: Composite handles resist weather and overstrikes and need little care. Some people prefer the feel of wood. Both work well when the head is sound.

faq.q: Can I split firewood with the A2400?
faq.a: Yes, for light splitting and kindling. For heavy firewood work, a dedicated splitting axe or maul is more efficient.

faq.q: How often should I sharpen my Husqvarna axe?
faq.a: Touch up the edge whenever it starts glancing instead of biting, and after any hit on dirt or stone.

name: Spencer 75 ft Logging Tape, 8ths, No Diameter
title: Spencer Loggers Tape, 75 ft, 8ths, No Diameter Scale
h1: Spencer 75 ft Loggers Tape, 8ths, No Diameter
meta: A Spencer loggers tape, 75 ft long and marked in 8ths with no diameter scale. Hook a log, walk back and buck to length fast. How to use it and keep it working.
tagline: Belt-mounted spring-return logging tape for bucking logs to length.
summary: This Spencer loggers tape is a 75 ft spring-return tape graduated in feet, inches and 8ths, with no diameter scale on the back. It clips to your belt, hooks into the end of a log and pays out as you walk, so a sawyer can measure and mark cuts without a helper.
highlights: 75 ft spring-return tape for bucking logs to length
Graduated in feet, inches and 8ths
No diameter scale, length markings only
Hook end bites into bark or the cut end of a log
Belt-mount case keeps hands free for the saw

p: A logging tape is built for one person working alone in the woods. The tape lives in a case on your belt, and the free end has a sharp hook or nail. Drive the hook into the end of the log, walk down the log, and the tape pays out behind you. When you reach the length you want, mark the cut with your saw. A flick of the tape pops the hook loose and the spring pulls it back into the case.

Spencer is the name most sawyers think of when they hear original loggers tape. Their tapes have been a standard on landings and in firewood yards for a long time, and parts and refills are easy to find.

The case is the part you will notice most. A good one sits flat on the belt, does not catch on brush and lets the tape pay out smoothly at any angle. Spencer cases are built for that kind of daily use, which is why many sawyers have been wearing the same case for years with just a refill or two.

This version is graduated in feet and inches down to eighths, which suits anyone cutting to specific lengths for sawlogs, firewood rounds or customer requests. It has no diameter scale on the reverse side. Diameter tapes are useful for timber cruising and scaling, but if you only buck to length, a plain length tape is simpler to read.

A 75 ft tape covers most bucking work on tree service jobs and in the woods. You can measure a full trunk on the ground and lay out several cuts in one walk, which saves trips back and forth with the saw running.

Accurate lengths matter more than people expect. A mill may dock or reject logs that come in short, and a firewood customer who asked for 16 inch rounds will notice when half of them are 20. A tape takes the guesswork out of eyeballing cuts against the bar.

On removals, a logging tape helps when a customer wants wood cut to set lengths, when you are bucking sawlogs for a mill, or when you are cutting to fit a trailer or a log truck. Mark cuts with a quick nick from the saw or a lumber crayon, then come back and buck.
Never measure a log that is moving, rolling or under tension, and keep the tape and your hands clear of the chain when someone else is bucking. Hook the tape, step back, then call the cut.
Clip the case where it does not interfere with your saw hand. Many sawyers wear it on a logging belt with their wedges and a file.

On big trunks, lay out every cut before you start the saw. It is faster to walk the log once with the tape and mark each length than to stop between cuts, and it lets you plan around crooks, forks and defects so you get the most usable wood.

Let the tape rewind under control instead of letting it snap back, which wears the hook and the spring. Wipe off mud and sap now and then, and keep the case out of the chipper chute. When the blade finally kinks or snaps, a refill puts it back to work without replacing the whole case. See the Spencer 50 ft refill and confirm the refill length matches your case before you order.

faq.q: What does 8ths mean on a loggers tape?
faq.a: The tape is marked in feet and inches with eighth-inch divisions, so you can measure lengths precisely.

faq.q: Do I need a diameter scale?
faq.a: Only if you scale or cruise timber. For bucking logs to length, a plain length tape is all you need.

faq.q: Can I replace the tape blade?
faq.a: Yes. Spencer sells refills. Match the refill length and type to your case.

name: Spencer Logging Tape Measure 35
title: Spencer Loggers Tape Measure 35: Belt Logging Tape
meta: The Spencer 35 loggers tape measure clips to your belt and hooks the end of a log so one person can measure cuts. Uses, features and care for a Spencer tape.
tagline: Belt-mounted Spencer loggers tape for one-person measuring on the landing.
summary: The Spencer 35 is a loggers tape measure designed for one person: it clips to your belt, the hook end grabs the log, and the tape pays out as you walk. It is a quick way to buck logs, firewood and sawlogs to consistent lengths.
highlights: Belt-mounted case keeps both hands free
Hook end grips the log so you can work alone
Spring return rewinds the tape after each measure
Made by Spencer, a long-time name in logging tapes
Refills available, so the case lasts for years
specs: Hook for log ends and bark

body.h: What makes a loggers measuring tape different
p: A regular construction tape measure needs a second person or a nail at the far end. A loggers tape solves that with a hook that bites into wood. You set the hook in the end of the log, walk away and the tape follows. Read the length, mark the cut and give the tape a flick to free the hook. The spring winds it back into the case on your belt.
That is why Spencer tapes are a fixture with fallers, firewood producers and tree crews who buck wood to length. The tape stays on your hip, so measuring takes seconds and does not slow down the saw.

It is also faster than any alternative. Pacing off a log or holding the bar against it to estimate length is fine for rough firewood, but it adds up to a lot of error over a day. A tape makes every cut repeatable.

Spencer makes tapes in several lengths and with different graduations, including versions with a diameter scale on the back for scaling and cruising. Check the listing for this model's length and markings and pick what fits your work. Shorter tapes are lighter on the belt and fine for firewood and short logs. Longer tapes, like the Spencer 75 ft tape, let you lay out several cuts along a whole trunk in one walk.
If you only need lengths, a tape without a diameter scale is easier to read. If you buy and sell timber by volume, a diameter scale saves carrying a second tool.

Wear the case where you can reach it easily but where it will not bang against the saw. Many sawyers put it on the back or off-hand hip of a logging belt. Set the hook firmly before you walk, keep the tape straight along the log and read the mark at the point you want to cut.
Never measure a log that is moving, rolling or under tension, and keep the tape and your hands clear of the chain when someone else is bucking. Hook the tape, step back, then call the cut.
When bucking for a mill, ask for their length specs and trim allowance before you start. A few inches of trim on every log saves a lot of arguing later.

Firewood cutters often measure once to set the length and then use a mark on the saw or a stick for the rest of the cuts. A tape is still useful for checking every so often that the cuts have not drifted long or short.

Let the tape rewind slowly rather than snapping back. Keep the hook sharp enough to grip. Clean off mud and pitch, and keep the case out of the dirt when you set it down. If the tape blade breaks or wears out, replace it with a refill instead of buying a new case. Confirm the refill fits your model first. Browse the rest of our forestry tools for scaling sticks and other measuring gear.
Store the tape in a dry spot when you are done for the day. A case left in a puddle in the truck bed can rust inside, and a rusty spring does not rewind well.

faq.q: How do you use a loggers tape?
faq.a: Set the hook in the end of the log, walk along the log as the tape pays out, read the length you want and mark the cut. Flick the tape to free the hook and let it rewind.

faq.q: Is a Spencer tape worth it over a cheap tape measure?
faq.a: For bucking logs alone, yes. The hook and belt-mount case let one person measure without help.

faq.q: Can I get a refill for my Spencer tape?
faq.a: Yes. Spencer sells refills in several lengths. Match the refill to your case model.

name: Spencer Logging Tape Measure 50 ft Refill
title: Spencer Loggers Tape Refill, 50 ft Replacement Blade
meta: A 50 ft refill for your Spencer loggers tape. Swap in a fresh blade when the old one kinks, breaks or wears out, and keep using the case you already own.
tagline: Replacement 50 ft blade that puts a worn Spencer logging tape back in service.
summary: This 50 ft refill replaces the blade in a Spencer loggers tape, so a kinked or broken tape does not mean buying a whole new case. It is the cheap way to keep a good logging tape working for years.
highlights: 50 ft replacement blade for Spencer logging tapes
Costs less than a complete new tape
Keeps your existing case and belt clip in service
Worth keeping a spare in the truck
Confirm fit with your case model before ordering
specs: Spencer cases that take a 50 ft refill

p: A logging tape blade lives a rough life. It gets stepped on, dragged over bark, run over by skidders and occasionally nicked by a saw. Eventually it kinks, the markings wear off, or it snaps. The case and spring, though, often have plenty of life left.

A refill lets you replace only the part that wore out. That saves money and keeps the case you already have set up on your belt. Many sawyers keep a spare refill in the truck so a broken tape does not stop a day of bucking.

A fresh blade also brings back clear markings. Old tapes get worn, faded and coated in pitch until the numbers are hard to read in low light. A new refill is easier to read quickly, which means fewer mistakes and faster bucking.

Spencer cases are built for specific tape lengths and blade types. A 50 ft refill fits cases designed for 50 ft tapes. It will not fit a case built for a different length. Check the model on your case and compare it with the listing before you order. If your tape has a diameter scale or particular graduations, make sure the refill matches what you want to read.
If you are not sure what case you have, look for the model number on the case or contact Spencer with a description. Getting the right refill the first time beats a return trip.
A 50 ft length suits most firewood work, short logs and tree service bucking. It is lighter and quicker to rewind than a long tape, and many sawyers find it the most practical size for everyday use.

Follow the instructions that come with the refill. In general, you open the case, remove the old blade, attach the new blade to the reel and wind it in under spring tension. Wear gloves and eye protection, because springs and blade edges can be sharp and can move suddenly when released. Take your time and keep track of small parts.
Once it is installed, pull the tape out a few times and let it rewind slowly to make sure it runs smoothly and the hook seats properly.
If the case itself is cracked, the spring is weak or the belt clip is broken, a new complete tape may be the better buy. A refill only makes sense when the case is still in good shape.

Let the tape rewind under control, wipe off mud and pitch, and avoid laying it across the cut line when someone is bucking. Keep the hook sharp enough to bite, and do not use the tape to pull or drag anything. A little care goes a long way.
Never measure a log that is moving, rolling or under tension, and keep the tape and your hands clear of the chain when someone else is bucking. Hook the tape, step back, then call the cut.
Do not have a tape yet? The Spencer 75 ft loggers tape and the Spencer 35 tape come complete with a case.

faq.q: Will this refill fit my Spencer tape?
faq.a: It fits Spencer cases built for a 50 ft refill. Check the model on your case and compare it with the listing.

faq.q: Is replacing the blade hard?
faq.a: It takes some patience. Follow the included instructions and wear gloves and eye protection, since the spring is under tension.

faq.q: Does the refill include the case?
faq.a: No. It is the replacement blade only.

name: Husqvarna Long Handle Hookaroon
title: Husqvarna Hookaroon, Long Handle: Move Logs Easier
meta: A Husqvarna hookaroon with a long handle for dragging, rolling and stacking logs and rounds without bending. How tree crews and firewood cutters put it to use.
tagline: Long-handled pick for dragging, flipping and stacking logs and firewood.
summary: A hookaroon, also called a pickaroon, is a handle with a pointed steel pick on the end, and this Husqvarna hookaroon has a long handle that keeps your back straight. Swing the pick into a log or round, then drag, roll or lift it without bending over or putting your hands near the wood.
highlights: Long handle for less bending and more leverage
Pointed steel pick bites into logs and rounds
Moves wood without grabbing it by hand
Useful for stacking, loading and feeding the splitter
Saves backs on firewood and cleanup days
specs: Dragging, rolling, stacking logs and firewood

p: On a removal, a lot of the day is spent moving wood: dragging rounds to the trailer, rolling logs into position for bucking, pulling pieces off the pile. Doing that by hand means bending, grabbing rough bark and getting fingers close to pinch points. A hookaroon puts a steel pick on the end of a handle so you can do the same work standing up.

Swing the pick into the end grain or side of a round and pull. The pick holds while you drag, flip or lift. A quick twist pops it free. Once you have used one, it is hard to go back to grabbing wood by hand.

It is also a safety tool. Keeping your hands off the wood keeps them away from pinch points between rounds, away from splinters and out from under a piece that shifts on the pile. Your back and your fingers both last longer.

Short pickaroons are fast for stacking and splitting, but you still have to bend down. The long handle on this Husqvarna hookaroon lets you reach farther and stay more upright, which matters when you are moving wood for hours. It also gives more leverage for rolling logs and turning big rounds.
For heavier rolling and lifting, a cant hook such as the LogRite cant hook is the better tool. Many crews carry both.

The extra reach also helps on steep ground. You can hook a round from above and guide it down without stepping into its path, and you can pull pieces out of a brush pile without climbing onto the pile.

Set the pick firmly before you pull, and pull with your legs and body rather than your back. Keep your feet out of the path of the wood you are moving. A round that breaks loose can roll fast. Be careful of the pick when you swing it. Know where your feet and your coworkers are, and never swing toward anyone.

Do not use the hookaroon as a pry bar against a heavy log under load. If something is too heavy to drag safely, bring a cant hook, a skidding tong, a log arch or the machine. Wear gloves and boots with good toe protection when moving wood.

Firewood producers use hookaroons to load splitters and stack cords. Tree crews use them to clean up rounds after a removal, feed big pieces to a log loader, and sort wood on the trailer. Homeowners cutting their own firewood use them to save their backs.

Keep the point reasonably sharp so it bites easily, check that the head is tight on the handle, and store it with the point covered or facing down so nobody gets hurt reaching into the truck. Browse more log handling tools for the right setup for your work.

Hookaroons also make quick work of sorting a mixed pile: pull the straight sawlog pieces one way, firewood rounds another and junk wood toward the chip pile. Keep the chipper area clear of tools, though. Nothing but brush should ever go near the infeed.

faq.q: What is the difference between a hookaroon and a pickaroon?
faq.a: They are names for the same kind of tool: a handle with a pointed pick for moving wood.

faq.q: Is a hookaroon the same as a cant hook?
faq.a: No. A cant hook has a pivoting hook and is used to roll heavy logs. A hookaroon is for dragging, lifting and positioning smaller pieces.

faq.q: Is a long handle better than a short one?
faq.a: A long handle means less bending and more leverage. A short handle is quicker for close work like stacking at a splitter.

name: LogRite Aluminum Handled Cant Hook
title: LogRite Cant Hook, Aluminum Handle: Roll Logs Easier
meta: The LogRite cant hook pairs a light aluminum handle with a steel hook to roll, turn and lift logs for bucking and loading. Sizing tips, uses and safe handling.
tagline: Lightweight aluminum cant hook for rolling and positioning logs.
summary: The LogRite cant hook uses an aluminum handle and a steel pivoting hook to grab a log and roll it with leverage instead of muscle. LogRite tools are made in the USA, and their cant hooks are a common sight with firewood cutters, sawyers and tree crews.
highlights: Aluminum handle that is light to carry and will not rot
Steel hook pivots to grip a range of log diameters
Rolls and turns logs for bucking and loading
Lifts the end of a log off the ground to prevent saw pinch
Made in the USA by LogRite

body.h: What a cant hook is for
p: A log on the ground almost never sits the way you want it. You need to roll it to cut the far side, turn it to get a clean buck, or get it off the dirt so the chain does not hit rocks. A cant hook makes that possible for one person. The hook bites the log, the handle gives you leverage, and a heavy log rolls with a steady pull.

LogRite builds its handles from aluminum instead of wood. That keeps the tool light enough to carry around the job all day and means the handle will not crack, rot or swell from sitting in a wet truck.

A cant hook also saves chains. Every time you finish a cut by pushing the bar through into the dirt, you dull the chain. Rolling the log a quarter turn with a cant hook lets you finish the cut from the top without touching the ground, and a sharp chain lasts all day instead of an hour.

Cant hooks are sized by handle length, and the right one depends on the logs you handle. Shorter handles are lighter and fine for firewood-sized logs. Longer handles give more leverage for big logs and let you work farther from the log. Check the listing for the size and the diameter range it handles, and choose for the bigger logs you see regularly.

Some LogRite cant hooks can be fitted with a timberjack, a small foot that lifts the end of the log off the ground. That keeps the bar out of the dirt when bucking and stops the log from pinching the saw. Check what is included before you order.

body.h: LogRite tools on a tree job
p: Tree crews use a cant hook to roll trunk sections so they can buck them without cutting into the dirt, to position logs for a loader or trailer, and to break apart a pile of rounds. Firewood producers use them to feed logs onto a buck stand or splitter. Mill owners use them on the deck.
For lighter wood and stacking, pair it with a LogRite hookaroon. For carrying logs between two people, look at the LogRite log carrier.

Always work from the uphill side of a log and make sure the path the log will roll is clear of people and your own feet. Set the hook firmly and pull steadily rather than jerking. If the hook slips, you want to fall away from the log, not toward it. A rolling log can crush a foot or leg in an instant.

Do not stand on logs you are rolling, and never put your hands under a log that is propped up. On steep ground, think through where the log will go before you move it. If a log is too big to move safely by hand, use equipment. Wear boots with good toe protection and keep the hook point sharp so it bites cleanly.
Keep your free hand off the log and away from the hook while rolling. If the log shifts unexpectedly, you want both hands on the handle and your body out of its path.

faq.q: What size LogRite cant hook should I get?
faq.a: Match the handle length to the logs you move most. Longer handles give more leverage for big logs; shorter handles are lighter for firewood.

faq.q: Are aluminum cant hooks strong enough?
faq.a: LogRite designs its aluminum handles for heavy log work. As with any tool, use it within its intended size range and do not use it as a lever under extreme loads.

faq.q: What is a cant hook handle made of?
faq.a: Traditional cant hooks use wood. LogRite uses aluminum, which is lighter for its strength and does not rot or crack from moisture.

name: LogRite Aluminum Handled Hookaroon
title: LogRite Hookaroon, Aluminum Handle: Drag and Stack Wood
meta: The LogRite hookaroon pairs a light aluminum handle with a hardened pick for dragging, flipping and stacking wood without bending. Uses, care and safe handling.
tagline: Aluminum-handled pickaroon for moving rounds, logs and firewood without bending.
summary: The LogRite hookaroon is a pickaroon with a lightweight aluminum handle and a steel pick that bites into wood so you can drag, lift and flip it without grabbing it by hand. It is made in the USA and built for people who move a lot of wood.
highlights: Aluminum handle that is light, strong and weatherproof
Steel pick that sets easily in end grain and bark
Drag, flip and stack wood without bending over
Keeps hands away from splinters and pinch points
Made in the USA by LogRite

p: Moving firewood and rounds is the part of the job nobody brags about, but it takes a lot of time and a lot of backs. A hookaroon cuts the bending in half. Swing the pick into a round, lift or drag it where it needs to go and pop it free.

LogRite uses aluminum for its handles, so the tool stays light enough to swing all day and will not crack or swell from weather. The pick is set to bite cleanly and release with a twist. Users tend to keep them for years.

It is also a good length for most people to use standing upright. You can reach a round a step away, pull it in and lift it to waist height without stooping, which adds up to a lot less strain over a day of splitting and stacking.

body.h: Where it fits on a crew
p: Tree crews use the LogRite hookaroon after a removal to sort rounds, drag pieces to the trailer and pull wood off the pile without climbing on it. Firewood producers use it to load splitters, toss split wood onto a conveyor and stack cords. Homeowners use it to move their own firewood without wrecking their backs.
For rolling heavy logs, a LogRite cant hook gives far more leverage. A hookaroon is the faster tool for everything smaller.

On storm jobs, where there is a lot of wood to clear quickly, a couple of hookaroons on the crew can noticeably speed up how fast a yard gets cleaned. Ground people spend less time bent over and more time moving wood.

Know where the pick will go before you swing it. Keep your feet and other people out of the way, and do not swing toward anyone. Set the point firmly before pulling so it does not pop out and send you off balance. Lift with your legs and keep your back straight.
Do not use it to pry heavy logs under load or as a hammer. Keep wood moving downhill under control, and stay out of the path of a round that could roll. Wear gloves and boots with toe protection.
Never use it near a running chipper or splitter's moving parts. Set the wood down where the operator can feed it safely.

Keep the point reasonably sharp with a file so it bites without having to swing hard. Check that the head is tight on the handle. Store it point-down or covered so nobody reaches into the truck and catches a hand on it. An aluminum handle needs little care beyond a wipe-down, but inspect it for dents or bends after a hard knock and replace it if it is damaged.
Mark your hookaroon with crew or company paint. They are popular tools and tend to wander off between jobs.
If the pick wears short or gets damaged from hitting rocks, check whether a replacement head is available before buying a whole new tool.

faq.q: Is a hookaroon the same as a pickaroon?
faq.a: Yes. Both names describe a handle with a pointed pick used to move wood.

faq.q: Why choose an aluminum handle?
faq.a: Aluminum is light, strong and does not rot, crack or swell like wood when left in the weather.

faq.q: Where are LogRite tools made?
faq.a: LogRite tools are made in the USA.

name: LogRite Log Carrier
title: LogRite Log Carrier: Two-Person Log Lifting Tool
meta: The LogRite log carrier lets two people grab and lift a log between them without bending or pinched fingers. How tree crews and firewood cutters use one.
tagline: Two-person log lifting tool with a center hook and aluminum handle.
summary: The LogRite log carrier is a tong-style hook on a long aluminum handle that lets two people lift and carry a log between them, one on each side. It is a simple tool that makes moving short logs safer and much easier on the back.
highlights: Two-person carry with a handle on each side
Self-gripping hook that tightens as you lift
Aluminum handle that stays light and weatherproof
Keeps hands away from the log and pinch points
Made in the USA by LogRite

p: Two people stand on either side of a log. The hook in the middle drops over the log and bites in, and each person grabs a side of the handle. When you lift, the weight closes the hook tighter on the log. Set the log down and the hook releases.

Instead of two people bending over and trying to get fingers under a log, both stand up straight with a solid grip. The log hangs low between you, which keeps the load near your body and easy to control.
The design works on a wide range of diameters because the hook closes as weight comes on. That is what makes it so quick to use: drop it on, lift, walk, set down and move on to the next log.

body.h: Where log carriers help on a tree job
p: Not every log needs a machine. Short trunk sections, long limbs and logs that need to go up a slope or through a gate to the trailer are classic log carrier work. On residential jobs where you cannot get equipment into the backyard, a pair of log carriers and four people can move a surprising amount of wood.

Firewood producers use log carriers to move logs from the pile to the buck stand. Woodworkers and sawyers with small mills use them to put logs onto the deck. Pair the carrier with a LogRite cant hook for rolling and a hookaroon for the small stuff.

It is also handy for moving logs in tight spots where you cannot roll them, like through a narrow side yard, over a fence line or onto a trailer ramp. Rolling a log is easy on open ground, but carrying it is the only option when you need control in close quarters.
Crews that do a lot of hand-carry work often keep two carriers on the truck. With four people and two carriers, longer logs can be moved with the weight shared evenly.

Agree on signals before you lift and set down: lift on three, stop, set it down. Lift with your legs, keep your back straight and walk at the same pace. Know the route before you pick up the log and clear trip hazards like branches and loose rounds.

Do not overload the carrier or try to carry a log that is too heavy for two people. If a log is too big to carry comfortably, cut it shorter, use two carriers with four people, or bring in equipment. Keep your feet clear of where the log would land if the hook let go. Wear gloves and boots with toe protection.

Check the hook and pivot for wear and damage before use, and keep the points sharp enough to bite. Wipe off sap and mud. The aluminum handle does not need much maintenance, but replace any part that is bent or cracked. Browse more log handling tools to round out your kit.
Store the carrier where the hook cannot catch on other gear or someone's hand. A simple hook on the trailer wall or a slot in a tool rack works well.

faq.q: How many people does a log carrier need?
faq.a: Two, one on each side of the handle. Very long logs can be carried with two carriers and four people.

faq.q: How heavy a log can I carry?
faq.a: Only what both people can lift comfortably and safely. When in doubt, cut the log shorter or use equipment.

faq.q: Does the hook damage the log?
faq.a: It leaves small marks where the points bite, which usually do not matter for firewood or sawlogs.

name: Husqvarna 230iB Battery Leaf Blower

tagline: Handheld 36 V battery blower for quiet, quick cleanup at the end of a job.
summary: The Husqvarna 230iB is a handheld battery-powered blower that runs on Husqvarna's 36 V battery system. It is a quiet, no-fuel way to clear sawdust, chips and leaves off driveways, decks and walkways at the end of a tree job.
highlights: Runs on Husqvarna 36 V batteries
No mixed fuel, no pull cord, instant start
Quieter than a gas blower for residential work
Light enough to use one-handed for cleanup
Shares batteries with other Husqvarna battery tools
specs: Check listing for what is included

body.h: Why tree crews carry a battery blower
p: Every tree job ends with cleanup: sawdust on the driveway, chips on the sidewalk, leaves and twigs on the patio. A battery blower handles that in a few minutes without the noise and fumes of a gas engine. That matters on residential jobs, early mornings and in neighborhoods with noise rules.
The 230iB is a handheld model, so it is easy to grab off the truck, clear a deck or a walkway and put back. There is no mixing fuel, no choke and no pull cord. Squeeze the trigger and it runs.

It also helps when the customer is home. Running a loud gas blower outside someone's window while they are on a call does not leave a good impression. A quieter battery blower lets you clean up without interrupting the household or the neighbors.

Runtime depends on the battery size and how hard you run it. A bigger BLi battery runs longer but adds weight. Most crews find a couple of batteries cover end-of-job cleanup across a day, especially if a charger rides in the truck. The Husqvarna QC500 charger recharges batteries quickly between jobs.

Because the 230iB uses the same 36 V batteries as Husqvarna's other battery tools, including the T540iXP top-handle saw, a crew can share packs across tools instead of carrying separate systems. Check the listing to see whether a battery and charger are included or the blower is tool-only.
Charging batteries in the truck on an inverter or at the shop overnight keeps the rotation simple: one pack in the blower, one charging, and one spare for the saw.

A gas blower still moves more air for long periods and is the better choice for big leaf jobs or clearing a large property. For the cleanup that follows tree work, a handheld battery blower is usually enough and much more pleasant to use. Many crews carry both: a gas or backpack blower for heavy work and a battery blower for quick cleanup and noise-sensitive jobs.
If you want a gas handheld instead, the Husqvarna 125B is a popular choice.
Battery blowers also need less maintenance: no spark plug, no carburetor and no fuel that goes stale. For a tool that may only run ten minutes a day, that is a big advantage.

Wear eye and hearing protection. Battery blowers are quieter than gas models, but they still kick up grit and debris. Do not point the blower at people, pets or cars, and watch for stones on gravel driveways. Keep the air intake clear of leaves and debris.

Store batteries indoors at moderate temperatures, keep them dry, and do not leave them baking on the dashboard in summer. Follow Husqvarna's manual for charging and storage, and inspect batteries for damage before use.

faq.q: What battery does the Husqvarna 230iB use?
faq.a: It runs on Husqvarna's 36 V BLi battery system, the same batteries used across their handheld battery line.

faq.q: Is the 230iB strong enough for leaves?
faq.a: It handles light leaves, sawdust and debris on hard surfaces well. For large leaf jobs, a gas or backpack blower moves more air for longer.

faq.q: Does the 230iB come with a battery?
faq.a: It depends on the listing. Some are sold as a kit and some as tool-only. Check before you order.

name: Husqvarna QC500 Quick Charge Battery Charger
title: Husqvarna Battery Charger QC500: Fast 36 V Charging
h1: Husqvarna QC500 Quick Charge Battery Charger
meta: The Husqvarna QC500 battery charger is a fast charger for 36 V BLi batteries. Keep saws and blowers running all day with a quick rotation of charged packs.
tagline: Fast charger for Husqvarna 36 V BLi batteries, built for crews that run all day.
summary: The QC500 is a Husqvarna battery charger built for speed. It charges the 36 V BLi batteries used in Husqvarna's battery saws, blowers and trimmers faster than the standard chargers, so a small set of batteries can keep tools running through a full workday.
highlights: Quick charger for Husqvarna 36 V BLi batteries
Higher output than the standard Husqvarna chargers
Keeps a battery rotation going on busy days
Works across the Husqvarna battery tool line
Good fit for the shop or a truck with a suitable power supply

p: With battery tools, the number of batteries you need depends on how fast you can charge them. A slow charger means buying extra packs to cover the day. A fast charger like the QC500 lets a smaller set of batteries rotate: one in the tool, one charging, one ready.

For a climber running a battery top-handle saw, that difference matters. A saw that goes dead halfway through a pruning job means a trip down the rope. With a quick charger in the truck or at the job site, the ground person can keep fresh packs ready to send up.

Fast charging also helps crews that are moving from gas to battery one tool at a time. If the blower, the pole saw and the top-handle all share packs, a quick charger keeps every tool topped up without buying a battery for each one.

The QC500 is made for Husqvarna's 36 V BLi battery packs, the same batteries used in their handheld battery tools such as the T540iXP top-handle saw and the 230iB blower. It does not charge batteries from other brands or other Husqvarna voltage systems.
Charge times depend on the battery size and its condition. Larger capacity batteries take longer. Check Husqvarna's charge time chart for your battery to plan how many you need for a day.

If you are building a battery kit from scratch, think about the whole day before you buy. Count how many tool-hours you run, how long each battery lasts in your work and how long the QC500 takes to refill it. That tells you whether two batteries are enough or you need three.

Many crews charge at the shop overnight and bring the charger along for longer days. If you charge from the truck, use an inverter or generator with enough clean power to run the charger, and make sure the setup is properly installed and protected. An undersized inverter can shut down or damage electronics.
Keep the charger dry and out of the chip and sawdust mess. A small box or a shelf inside the cab or utility body keeps it clean and ventilated. Do not cover the vents while it is running.
Set up the charging spot so batteries are easy to swap without climbing into the truck. A labeled shelf for charged and empty packs saves confusion when several people are using the same batteries.

Let hot batteries cool a little before charging if the charger asks for it. Store batteries and charger at moderate temperatures. Heat and freezing cold both shorten battery life. Do not charge damaged, swollen or wet batteries, and keep contacts clean. Follow the manual for long-term storage, and inspect cords and plugs regularly. Replace a charger with a damaged cord rather than taping it.

A battery that suddenly runs for much less time than it used to may be near the end of its life. Track the age and condition of your packs, and retire damaged ones properly through a battery recycling program rather than the trash.

faq.q: Which batteries does the Husqvarna QC500 charge?
faq.a: It charges Husqvarna 36 V BLi batteries used in their handheld battery tools.

faq.q: Is the QC500 faster than the standard Husqvarna charger?
faq.a: Yes. It is Husqvarna's quick charger with higher output than the standard models. Actual times depend on the battery size.

faq.q: Can I charge from my truck?
faq.a: Yes, with an inverter or generator that can supply enough clean power for the charger. Check the charger's input requirements.

name: Husqvarna T540iXP Top Handle Battery Chainsaw Kit
title: Husqvarna T540iXP Battery Chainsaw: Top Handle Kit
h1: Husqvarna T540iXP Top Handle Battery Chainsaw Kit
meta: The Husqvarna T540iXP is a top handle battery chainsaw built for arborists working in the tree. What the kit includes, who should run it and how it compares.
tagline: Professional 36 V top-handle saw for trained climbers working aloft.
summary: The T540iXP is the Husqvarna battery chainsaw built for arborists: a 36 V top-handle saw designed for pruning and dismantling work in the tree. This kit pairs the saw with battery power so a climber can go up without fuel, a pull cord or exhaust fumes.
highlights: Top-handle design for trained arborists working in the tree
Runs on Husqvarna 36 V BLi batteries
No fuel, no pull start, instant on and off
Quieter than gas, good for residential and early starts
Lanyard ring for securing the saw to your saddle
Kit format; check listing for included battery and charger

p: Top-handle saws are made for one job: cutting in the tree by a trained arborist who is tied in and in a secure work position. The compact layout lets a climber handle the saw close to the body in tight spots. That same layout makes them unsafe for general ground use by untrained users, and ANSI Z133 and manufacturer instructions limit how they should be used. If you are not a trained climber, buy a rear-handle saw.

For working arborists, the T540iXP brings battery power to the canopy. It is one of the most popular battery top-handle saws on tree crews and a favorite for pruning, crown work and small dismantling cuts.

body.h: Why go battery in the tree
p: Pulling a cold gas top-handle in the tree is a nuisance at best. A battery saw starts with a trigger every time. There is no fuel to spill on your gear, no exhaust in your face in a tight crown and much less noise for you, the ground crew and the neighbors. Between cuts the chain stops and the saw is silent, which makes communication with the ground easier.

The trade-off is runtime and top-end power on big wood. For heavy dismantling with large cuts, many climbers still send a gas saw up. For pruning, deadwooding and everyday climbing work, a battery top-handle covers most of the day with a battery swap or two.

Battery saws also need less routine care. There is no carburetor to tune, no spark plug, no air filter to clog with sawdust and no fuel to go stale. Keep the chain sharp, the bar oiled and the battery contacts clean, and the saw is ready to go.

The saw runs on Husqvarna's 36 V BLi batteries, shared with their other battery tools. Larger batteries run longer but add weight on your saddle, so many climbers use a mid-size pack for balance. Keep a fresh battery on the ground and send it up in a bag when needed. A Husqvarna QC500 quick charger keeps the rotation moving on long days.
Kit contents vary by seller. Check the listing to see which battery, which charger and which bar and chain are included before comparing prices.
Remember that the saw still needs bar and chain oil. Check the oil level every time you swap a battery so the bar never runs dry aloft.

Always secure the saw to your saddle with a saw lanyard. Cut with two hands whenever possible and keep the chain brake engaged when you move. Plan each cut so the saw and your lifeline are never in the same path. Your climbing system, including rope and saddle, must meet the applicable standard and be inspected before every climb.
Wear a helmet with eye and hearing protection, cut-resistant gloves where appropriate and saw protection for your legs. Get trained by a qualified arborist before using a top-handle saw aloft.
Keep the chain sharp. A dull chain makes any saw grab and kick, and a battery saw with a dull chain also drains the battery faster. Many climbers touch up the chain at every battery change.

faq.q: Is the Husqvarna T540iXP good for homeowners?
faq.a: No. Top-handle saws are designed for trained arborists working in trees. For ground use, choose a rear-handle saw.

faq.q: How long does the battery last?
faq.a: It depends on the battery size, the wood and how you cut. Most climbers carry at least one spare battery for a full day.

faq.q: Can I use other Husqvarna batteries in the T540iXP?
faq.a: It uses Husqvarna's 36 V BLi batteries. Check the manual for the recommended battery models.

faq.q: What bar length does the T540iXP use?
faq.a: It is commonly run with a 12 or 14 in bar. Check the kit listing for the bar and chain included.

name: Husqvarna 125B Handheld Blower
title: Husqvarna 125B Handheld Blower: Specs and Buying Guide
meta: The Husqvarna 125B is a 28 cc handheld gas blower for cleaning up sawdust, chips and leaves after tree work. Specs, fuel, maintenance and how it compares.
tagline: 28 cc handheld gas blower for fast cleanup on tree jobs and around the yard.
summary: The Husqvarna 125B is a 28 cc handheld gas blower that has been a common sight on landscape and tree service trucks for years. It is light enough to use one-handed and strong enough to clear sawdust, chips and leaves from driveways, patios and lawns.
highlights: 28 cc 2-stroke engine
Runs on 50:1 mixed fuel
Handheld design for quick cleanup
Cruise control to hold engine speed
Simple to maintain and widely serviced

body.h: A cleanup blower for tree crews
p: After a removal, the yard has to look better than when you arrived. The 125B is the kind of blower that lives on the truck for exactly that: clear sawdust from the driveway, chips from the sidewalk and leaves from the patio, then put it away. It is a handheld, so it is easy to grab, light to carry and quick to start.
It runs on standard 50:1 mixed fuel, the same mix most crews already carry for their saws. That means one fuel can covers the blower and the 2-stroke saws.
Climbers also use it to clear sawdust off the trunk and ground before rigging a big piece, so the ground crew can see the landing zone and footing clearly. A clean work area is a safer work area.

The 125B moves plenty of air for its size and weight, which is why so many landscapers and tree crews have used one. It has a cruise control so you can set the engine speed and give your trigger finger a break on long cleanups. Controls are simple, and parts and service are widely available through Husqvarna dealers.
For big leaf jobs and large properties, a backpack blower moves more air for longer with less arm fatigue. For quick cleanup after tree work, a handheld is the faster tool to pull off the truck.
Being a handheld also means it fits in the truck box with the saws, instead of taking up a whole spot like a backpack unit. For crews with limited space, that alone makes it worth having.

Use fresh gas mixed at 50:1 with quality 2-stroke oil, such as Husqvarna XP oil, or ethanol-free premix. Old fuel is the number one reason handheld blowers will not start. If the blower will sit for more than a few weeks, run it on premix or drain the fuel.

Clean the air filter regularly, since blowers pull in a lot of dust. Check the spark plug and spark arrestor screen per the manual. A clogged screen makes the engine lose power. Keep the intake clear of leaves and debris, and never run it without the intake guard.
At the end of the season, run the blower on premix before storing it, or drain the tank and run the carburetor dry. Store it in a clean, dry spot and it will start easily in spring.

Wear eye and hearing protection, and a dust mask in dry, dusty conditions. Do not point the blower at people, pets or vehicles, and watch for gravel and small stones that can become projectiles. Refuel with the engine off and cool, away from where you will start it. If you prefer a quieter option for residential work, compare it with the Husqvarna 230iB battery blower.
Use the blower at lower throttle near beds and mulch so you move debris without scattering mulch everywhere. Work in one direction toward a pile or the curb rather than blowing debris back and forth.

faq.q: What fuel mix does the Husqvarna 125B use?
faq.a: It runs on gasoline mixed with 2-stroke oil at 50:1.

faq.q: What is the engine size of the 125B?
faq.a: The Husqvarna 125B has a 28 cc 2-stroke engine.

faq.q: Why won't my 125B start?
faq.a: The most common causes are old fuel, a dirty air filter, a fouled spark plug or a clogged spark arrestor screen. Start with fresh fuel and work through the manual's troubleshooting steps.
